papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Classifiers for Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection Using Feature Reduction
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems can improve IoT security, but high-dimensional traffic features and imbalanced datasets may reduce model reliability and deployment feasibility in resource-constrained environments. This study presents a lightweight binary IoT intrusion detection framework using an approximately balanced CICIoT2023 derived dataset, feature reduction, and comparative machine learning evaluation. The original multi-class attack labels were converted into two classes: Benign and Malicious. To reduce class bias, malicious traffic was randomly undersampled to obtain an approximately balanced binary dataset. Information Gain Ratio and Gini Decrease were then used to rank traffic features and generate reduced feature subsets of 38, 30, 20, 10, 5, and 3 features. Five machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest(RF), Decision Tree(DT), Naive Bayes(NB), Logistic Regression(LR), and Support Vector Machine(SVM), were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that Random Forest achieved the strongest overall performance. In particular,the 20-feature subset achieved accuracy of 99.1% and MCC of 0.982, matching the full-feature model while reducing feature dimensionality by approximately 47.4%. The 10-feature subset also maintained strong performance with accuracy of 98.9% and MCC of 0.979, reducing the feature space by approximately 73.7%. These findings demonstrate that balanced binary classification and progressive feature reduction can preserve detection effectiveness while improving lightweight IDS feasibility.

papers.title: Arcadian: Open-Source Humanoid Ecosystem for Accessible and Customizable Research and Education
papers.abstract: Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support. This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support. Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education. Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility. Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks. The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build. All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates. The ecosystem resources are available at https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.

papers.title: FL-CsLoc-DH: A Federated Learning-Based Crowdsensing Localization under Dual Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Mobile Crowdsensing (MCS) provides a scalable way to collect indoor fingerprints and reduce professional calibration effort. To protect the location privacy of participating clients, Federated Learning (FL) is used so that raw fingerprints and measurement trajectories remain local. However, owing to the open and uncontrollable nature of MCS, participating clients collect fingerprints in different propagation environments and possess unequal labeling availability. These conditions jointly cause data and annotation heterogeneity, which degrades FL-based crowdsensing localization. In this work, we propose FL-CsLoc-DH, a federated semi-supervised learning framework for crowdsensing localization under dual heterogeneity. FL-CsLoc-DH coordinates Two-Stage Noisy Gradient Rejection (TS-NGR), Soft Fisher Confidence Alignment (S-FCA), and Trajectory-Smoothed Model Averaging (T-SMA) throughout localization model learning. TS-NGR suppresses unreliable client updates caused jointly by environment dependent data shifts and noisy pseudo labels. S-FCA limits parameter increments dominated by unlabeled data, thereby alleviating annotation heterogeneity during local training. T-SMA smooths the aggregated global localization model trajectory to reduce drift induced by data heterogeneity. Experiment results show that the three mechanisms provide complementary improvements in localization accuracy under the MCS environment while retaining raw client data locally.

papers.title: Sharp integral Ricci pinching on manifolds with positive total scalar curvature
papers.abstract: Let $(M,g)$ be a closed connected Riemannian three-manifold with $\int_M R \mathrm{d}v>0$, and assume that $M$ is not diffeomorphic to a spherical space form. We prove the sharp integral Ricci pinching inequality $$\mathrm{vol}(g)\int_M |\mathrm{Ric}^{\circ}|^2 \mathrm{d}v \geq \frac{1}{6}\left(\int_M R \mathrm{d}v\right)^2.$$ Moreover, equality holds if and only if $(M,g)$ is locally isometric to $\mathbb{S}^2(a)\times\mathbb{R}$ for some $a>0$. By the same method, we prove $\mathrm{vol}(g)\int_M |\mathrm{Ric}^{\circ}|^2 \mathrm{d}v \geq \frac{1}{12}\left(\int_M R \mathrm{d}v\right)^2$ on closed four-manifolds with $\int_M R \mathrm{d}v>0$ that have a finite cover with positive first Betti number, and we provide a new proof of Gursky's inequality. We also show that the corresponding inequality fails in every dimension $n\geq 5$, and we give a metric on $\mathbb{S}^2\times\mathbb{S}^1$ that disproves a conjecture of Ge, Li and Lian.

papers.title: Characterizing Frozen SSL Encoders and Backends for Cross-Domain Speech Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders are the dominant front end for speech deepfake detection, and the prevailing recipe fine-tunes the full encoder on a small spoofing corpus, maximizing in-domain accuracy at the cost of known degradation under domain shift. Taking a recent cross-attention fusion of SSL and constant-Q cepstral features as a fixed reference recipe, we freeze its encoder and ask which encoder and which backend behave best across domains. We cross two frozen encoders, the massively multilingual XEUS and Wav2Vec2 XLSR-53, with two backends, multi-head factorized attentive (MHFA) pooling and AASIST, and evaluate on ASVspoof 2019 LA, ASVspoof 2021 LA and DF, In-the-Wild (ITW), and ASVspoof 5, training every system in one pipeline over three seeds. We report three findings. First, encoder and backend interact: MHFA suits the stronger encoder, while AASIST recovers more from and stabilizes the weaker one. Second, within this recipe, the frozen encoder produces large, repeatable differences. With MHFA, frozen XEUS lowers error relative to frozen XLSR-53 by 58-77% on LA21, DF21, and ASV5, and more modestly on ITW. This ordering persists in a matched-aggregation ablation, and a capacity-matched WavLM Large diagnostic shows that parameter count alone does not explain XLSR-53's weaker performance. Third, against a three-seed fine-tuned baseline, frozen XEUS updates under 0.4M parameters versus 316M, wins on ASVspoof 5 (in EER and min-DCF) and modestly on LA21, trails on DF21 and ITW, and shows lower seed variation on three of the four out-of-domain sets.

papers.title: Grothendieck--Serre for quasi-split groups over two-dimensional regular local rings
papers.abstract: We prove the Grothendieck--Serre conjecture for quasi-split reductive group schemes over two-dimensional regular local rings, that is, every generically trivial torsor under a quasi-split group scheme $G$ over a regular local ring $R$ of dimension two is trivial. Our main result is new when $R$ is ramified and generalizes Nisnevich's result by removing the assumption that the residue field is infinite. By formal patching of torsors and valuative criteria, we are reduced to showing a product formula when $G$ is semisimple and simply connected. Then, we take advantage of relative simple reflections and relative Bruhat decomposition to prove a generation by rank-one subgroups. The analysis on Dynkin diagrams with Galois actions reduces us to $\operatorname{SL}_2$ and three-dimensional $\operatorname{SU}$ factors. For the special unitary case, we treat Hermitian forms by using stabilizations and cancellation to finish the proof.

papers.title: Sharp constant off-diagonal extrapolation for Muckenhoupt bases
papers.abstract: In this paper we prove a sharp constant version of off-diagonal extrapolation for matrix weights, improving the result we proved in an earlier paper. In an appendix, we give a new and simpler proof of this result in the scalar case.

papers.title: Exceptional Rays of Invariant Processes on Trees
papers.abstract: Let $A$ be an ergodic, non-constant random process on the $d$-regular tree $T_d$, with marginal distribution $X$. We prove that there always exist "exceptional" rays, whose asymptotic means are at least $\mathbb{E}(X)+δ$; furthermore, for edge processes, $δ> 0$ can be taken to depend only on the law of $X$. We compare different definitions of "maximal asymptotic means", relating them to different notions of speed of tree-indexed random walks.

papers.title: Where does pancreatic lesion segmentation fail on public CT? An attenuation-stratified analysis of a duct-guided pipeline on PanTS
papers.abstract: Lesion segmentation is a building block of most CT pipelines for pancreatic cancer detection, yet lesion overlap scores stay low. Instead of proposing a new architecture, we report where an end-to-end pipeline fails on a large public dataset. On PanTS we built a three-stage pipeline: pancreas segmentation, maps of the main pancreatic duct (MPD) and common bile duct (CBD), and a lesion model that receives the CT with or without the predicted duct maps. Both lesion models were trained identically on 4007 scans and evaluated once on 737 held-out test scans (127 with a lesion) under a comparison rule fixed before the test run. Lesion Dice was 0.213 with duct maps and 0.209 with CT only (paired difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.011 to +0.019). The duct maps raised the share of lesions touched by a prediction (+0.079, 95% CI +0.024 to +0.134) but also enlarged predictions in lesion-free scans, and lesion-like regions were predicted in all lesion-free test scans. Out of fold, keeping only the predicted components that touched the lesion raised Dice only from 0.285 to 0.309; the loss came mainly from the extent of correctly located predictions. Clearly hypoattenuating lesions, which intensity alone separates from normal pancreas, had the lowest coverage (median 16.6%). From the predicted maps alone, the MPD diameter separated lesion from lesion-free test scans with AUC 0.794 (95% CI 0.747 to 0.839), while the CBD diameter was weak (AUC 0.603) and added nothing. Code for training, inference and evaluation is publicly available.

papers.title: Cylindrical dimers and monomial immanants
papers.abstract: For a bipartite graph on a cylinder, group its perfect matchings by homological height and sum their weights in each group. We prove that every minor of the resulting Toeplitz matrix has nonnegative coefficients in the edge weights, settling a question recorded by Lai. We first prove conjectures of Galashin and the author concerning directed cycles in cylindrical networks, and then deduce the dimer theorem from them. A related, stronger positivity property for superpositions of cylindrical matchings turns out to be equivalent to Stembridge's interval-product conjecture on monomial immanants. Using annular webs, we prove this conjecture for partitions with at most four columns. A stretching argument extends this to all partitions with parts in $\{n,2n,3n,4n\}$.

papers.title: Semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash on H5N1 One Health questions
papers.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information during outbreaks. Before a chatbot's accuracy can be meaningfully assessed, its consistency must first be understood, so that any single response can be trusted as a fair representative of the model's behavior. We characterized the semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 (OpenAI) and Gemini 3 Flash (Google) on 15 H5N1 One Health questions sourced from social media discourse by adopting and extending a centroid-based evaluation framework. Each question was submitted 30 times and reformulated using five Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variants with 30 runs each, yielding 5,400 responses. Pairwise cosine similarity was computed on MPNet embeddings, with sensitivity analyses across three additional transformers. Statistical inference combined standard nonparametric tests (paired Wilcoxon and Friedman with Holm--Bonferroni correction) with inter-embedding agreement statistics (ICC(2,k) and Cronbach's $α$) introduced here as a methodological addition. Both models produced high mean consistency (0.93--0.97, rescaled to {[}0, 1{]}). GPT-5 showed reproducibility significantly higher than repeatability (W = 3.0, p = 0.0003), whereas for Gemini 3 Flash the two metrics were statistically indistinguishable (W = 42.0, p = 0.33). Differential Diagnosis ranked among the top two CoT framings for consistency in both models. The tested chatbots behave as semantically stable sources on H5N1 One Health questions, and the developed consistency evaluation framework is portable to other domains.

papers.title: Electric polarizabilities with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: While projector quantum Monte Carlo methods are known for producing accurate ground-state energies, the prediction of other properties that encode the electronic response to applied electric and magnetic fields has historically been challenging. In this work we demonstrate that the electric (static) polarizability tensor, which is formally a second-derivative of the energy with respect to electric fields, can be efficiently computed with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo using a correlated sampling finite-difference strategy. With simple Hartree-Fock trial wave functions, we investigate a series of small molecules (some of which are difficult for approximate density functionals), polyacenes of increasing size, and ferrocene as a representative organometallic complex. The methodology is scalable to relatively large molecules involving thousands of basis functions, and with appropriate trial wave functions remains robust for strongly correlated electronic states, as we show for the stretched dinitrogen molecule. This work opens the door to the computation of a host of other second-order molecular properties with auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo, which will inform the ongoing search for optimal trial wave functions and extend benchmark-quality training data sets for the refinement of semi-empirical and machine learning models for quantum chemistry and molecular simulation.

papers.title: Context-Aware Proactive Self-Adaptation: A Two-Layer Model Predictive Control Approach
papers.abstract: In self-adaptive software systems, the role of context is paramount, especially for proactive self-adaptation. Current research, however, does not fully explore context's impact, for example on priorities of the requirements. To address this gap, we introduce a novel contextual goal model to capture these factors and their influence on the system. Using this, we propose a two-layer control mechanism with a context-aware model predictive control to achieve proactive adaptation for the software system and adaptation for the controller itself. By contextual prediction and a more accurate system model, our approach utilizes model predictive control to facilitate timely and efficient system adaptations, improving both performance and adaptability. Meanwhile, we perform requirement adaptation to update the contextual goal model, which in turn updates the objective function and constraints of the controller. Our experimental evaluations across two scenarios demonstrate the significant benefits of our approach in enhancing system performance.

papers.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
papers.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

papers.title: Global classification and local asymptotics for a Monge-Ampère obstacle problem
papers.abstract: Let $n\geq2$ and $0<q<n$. We prove that every nontrivial convex entire solution of $$\det D^2v = v^q, \quad v \geq 0, \quad \text{in } \mathbb{R}^n$$ with bounded (possibly empty) coincidence set $\{v=0\}$ is affine equivalent to a radial solution. Together with the classification for unbounded coincidence sets by Jin-Tu-Xiong \cite{JTX2025}, this completes the classification of nontrivial nonnegative convex entire solutions. The proof uses an affine-invariant monotonicity formula extending the two-dimensional formula in Mooney-Sen \cite{MooneySen2026}. Combining this global classification with level-set parametrization and spectral analysis, we also obtain precise asymptotics of local solutions at isolated zeros, settling the remaining case, namely, a singleton free boundary, in the regularity theory for the Monge-Ampère obstacle problem studied in \cite{JTX2025}.

papers.title: Tight Query Depth of Recursive Randomized Greedy MIS
papers.abstract: The randomized greedy maximal independent set (RGMIS) algorithm processes vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily constructs an MIS. Its recursive formulation decides whether a vertex belongs to this MIS by querying lower-ranked neighbors in increasing rank order, stopping when a neighbor in the MIS is found. We prove that, on every $n$-vertex graph, this recursive algorithm has $O(\log n)$ query depth with high probability, even without memoization. The bound holds simultaneously for all starting vertices and is asymptotically tight even on bipartite graphs. The proof combines a bound on the total expected number of query paths with an exposure argument: paths with many two-edge shortcuts are unlikely, while the remaining paths admit sufficiently many applications of a two-hop probability bound.

papers.title: Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance the usability and reliability of LLMs, emphasizing the ongoing importance of well-designed prompts in optimizing task performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of prompt patterns in maximizing LLM's potential, even as their capabilities continue to evolve.

papers.title: GlobalHRBench: Does Changing the Question Language Change the Legal Answer?
papers.abstract: Language matters when deploying LLM agents across borders, especially in law, where the governing rules must hold across working languages. Does changing the language of a legal question change answer accuracy? We introduce GlobalHRBench, pairing 240 employment-law problems across eight jurisdictions and eight languages while fixing facts, applicable law and required conclusions. We evaluate nine models on all 1,920 prompts in independent, closed-book, single-answer trials, scoring legal correctness, completeness and answer-language compliance. GPT-6.1 Sol leads at 76.2% strict passes, with a 5.8% relative best-to-worst language decline, compared with 42.2% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Kimi K3.1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 5.5 reverse order between English and Chinese. A four-model study on 16 paired families compares closed-book answers with governing evidence, added cross-jurisdiction distractors and removal of a governing passage. Governing evidence corrects legal errors and shortens reasoning on recovered answers, yet recognizing an evidence gap does not ensure correct application of the rules that remain. These findings motivate multilingual training for accurate, efficient and evidence-supported answers, and deployment evaluation in the user's working language.

papers.title: LexiDet-OVD: Benchmarking Lexical Sensitivity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detectors localize objects from free-form text prompts, but their reliability depends on how users describe the target. Standard evaluations usually test a fixed class name, leaving prompt-induced failure modes underexplored. We introduce LexiDet-OVD, a benchmark and metric suite for studying lexical sensitivity in open-vocabulary object detection. We organize prompt sets into equivalent, conditional, and broad semantic scopes, and evaluate four detector families on fixed COCO and LVIS samples, each covering 30 classes (800 held-out COCO images and 1,000 LVIS images). Beyond mean and worst-prompt AP50, we report P10, CVaR at 20%, leave-one-prompt-out influence, detection agreement, box consistency, and confidence variance using one-to-one multi-instance matching. Equivalent-prompt best-to-worst gaps range from 5.3 to 23.4 points on COCO1000 and from 5.1 to 29.9 points on LVIS1000-30c, showing that strong average accuracy and lexical stability are distinct properties. We compare maximum-score selection, weighted-box fusion, Prompt Consensus, and an exploratory fusion rule. Aggregation recovers performance in several settings, but no method dominates all model-dataset pairs. A controlled Detic/SHiNe comparison further shows that semantic hierarchy enrichment does not by itself eliminate lexical sensitivity. These results support reporting prompt-distribution robustness alongside conventional open-vocabulary detection accuracy.

papers.title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
papers.abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

papers.title: A Positron Spectral Dip near 20 GV in Selected Orbital Projections of AMS-02 Data
papers.abstract: We analyze more than a decade of public Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) data (2011-2021), matching daily electron and positron spectra to the orbital record on 3268 common dates. For each sky window we weight the spectra by the time the orbital zenith spends there and divide each rigidity bin by its all-date mean. At 16.6-22.8 GV, the normalized positron flux dips below its neighboring bins in several projections. At the Galactic center and the Crab, the positron dip exceeds the electron dip by $3.04\pm1.19$ and $3.57\pm1.22$ percentage points, respectively (statistical errors). A scan centered on 1177 Fermi-LAT catalog sources also finds dips at PKS~0301$-$243 and PKS~1424+240. At fixed rigidity, 13.8\% of trials that shift the spectra relative to the orbit produce a dip somewhere in the catalog at least as deep as the observed maximum. An isotropic intensity with the measured daily spectra reproduces every projection exactly. In a zenith pencil-beam model, direct positron annihilation on a common cold-electron column at the Galactic center and the Crab produces less than 0.10 percentage points of dip depth in either projection.

papers.title: Circle-Pattern Linear Systems for the Twenty Trivalent Delaunay Types of a Genus-Two Surface: Rank, Feasibility and Polytope Dimension
papers.abstract: The hyperelliptic quotient of a closed genus-two Riemann surface is a hyperbolic sphere with six cone points of angle pi. Its Delaunay triangulation T is dual to a trivalent Voronoi graph G of one of twenty combinatorial types. For each type we study the angle system Ax = 1, x >= 0, where A is the vertex-edge incidence matrix of T and pi x_e is the angle subtended at a cone point by the Voronoi edge dual to e, equivalently the intersection angle of the two circumcircles adjacent across e. We prove that rank A = 6 for all twenty types, including the six whose triangulation has a loop, so the affine solution space always has the dimension of Teichmuller space. The polytope P = {Ax = 1, x >= 0} behaves differently. It is six-dimensional for exactly ten types, the ten Delaunay-realizable ones. For nine types it has dimension one, two or three, because non-negativity forces some wedge angles to vanish, and for the type of signature (2,2,2,2,8,8) it is empty. We show that five of the nine and the empty type never occur as Delaunay triangulations, and that the other four occur only as triangulations of non-trivalent Delaunay decompositions. Every vertex of every P is half-integral, as for fractional perfect matching polytopes. For the ten full-dimensional types every facet x_e = 0 lies at an edge where the Whitehead move is admissible, though not conversely, and the move identifies the facets of the two polytopes; these identifications pair the facet orbits of the ten cells under their automorphism groups. The free unfolding of the gluing grows at rate about 7.093. All finite statements are checked by an independent program, and the rank, infeasibility, forced coordinates, dimensions, vertices and facets are verified in Lean 4.

papers.title: MobileGrail: Learning Compact Guardrails for On-Device deployable Mobile GUI Agent Safety
papers.abstract: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.

papers.title: When Source-Domain Validation Fails to Transfer: A Staged Study of Hyperparameter Selection
papers.abstract: Hyperparameters for an unseen domain are often selected using held-out examples from the available source domains. Withholding entire source domains during validation seems to better reflect deployment shift, but does this produce better selections on independent targets? We investigate this question through two complementary studies. A preliminary factorial experiment crosses particle swarm optimization and random search with pooled source validation and a leave-one-source-domain-out mean-minimum fitness on PACS and Multi-Domain Sentiment. The domain-aware fitness does not provide a consistent target advantage. We then separate selector development from confirmation using a shared pool of 64 configurations per task across four image benchmarks. Complete target-performance landscapes on VLCS and Office-Home inform one rule: retain the top 16 configurations by pooled source validation, then select the largest leave-one-source-domain-out mean-minus-standard-deviation score. The rule is frozen before evaluation on TerraIncognita and SVIRO. Across their 14 target domains, its equal-dataset-weighted balanced-accuracy difference from pooled validation is +0.097 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-0.685, +0.960]), with five wins and nine losses. Exploratory analyses reveal substantial variation across datasets, target domains, and training seeds. These results do not establish equivalence or a general failure of domain-aware validation. They show that the evaluated source-domain criteria did not establish reliable target gains under the tested protocols, and motivate assessing selection rules on datasets independent of those used to develop them.

papers.title: Quantum-Memory Forensics for Tampered Quantum Seals: Resource-Dependent Sample Gains
papers.abstract: Quantum seals reveal that an object was disturbed, but not where, with which tool, or when the tool changed. We study quantum-memory forensics for sealed items returning through an untrusted network where one tool opens many. Each seal cell is half of a Bell pair whose partner the verifier keeps in a protected quantum memory, a secret Pauli frame turns any attack into a Pauli channel, and a three-tier report localizes the tampering, learns a hidden-parity fingerprint of the tool and detects a tool switch in arrival order, not necessarily in attack order. Attribution concerns attackers who do not erase that fingerprint, which a random Pauli layer would do cheaply. Each result is stated within one of four verifier classes. For per-unit verifiers, which never couple two seal units and hold no untouched reference, the sample separation is asymptotically exponential, by reduction from a known lower bound for one parity of strength up to 1/3. On ten tampered cells it is proved to be at least \qnProvedUniformMin-fold against non-adaptive stabilizer probes and observed in simulation at \qnEoneRatioFine-fold. Against an implemented self-referencing strategy the simulated gain is about twice the inverse squared strength. The value also depends on the attack: destroying the untouched cells makes the reference necessary, whereas copying errors exposes the fingerprint to reference-free probes. We derive the vault's qubit inventory and simulate a seal requirement curve: ten times more seal noise lengthens the seal's lifetime \qnSealLifeGainFive-fold at \qnSealRhoFive{} times the attribution cost at $r=10$.

papers.title: Second Moment Penny Packings via Rolling Spaces
papers.abstract: We solve the unrestricted minimum second moment problem for six unit disks in the plane by proving that the minimum is \(29/3\) attained uniquely up to isometry and relabelling by one disk together with five of its six neighbours in the triangular lattice. The realised contacts themselves define the space of admissible motions, while the directions preserving those contacts to first order define the rolling space consisting of motions whose relative velocities have zero normal component at every realised contact. Together, these spaces lead to an exact tangent cone formula and to a criterion by which a strictly positive centroidal contact balance, combined with rolling rigidity, implies strict local minimality modulo Euclidean motions. Our method recovers the classical five disk minimum \(34/5\) of Graham and Sloane, previously the largest unrestricted case known exactly. Geometric reductions and a graph census reduce the global search to finitely many contact graph classes. Exact analysis and validated interval arithmetic then exclude competing configurations, establishing the global bounds and uniqueness. Our method allows us to pass from putative lattice extremisers to unrestricted optimality.

papers.title: The Temporal Residual: Fast and Effective Retrofitting of Latent Feedback into Pretrained Language Models
papers.abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.

papers.title: Is Classical Error Control Ready for IMT-2030? Information-Loss Interfaces in Channel Estimation, FEC, CRC, and ARQ for Machine-Type Services
papers.abstract: Fault tolerance and structured error control in mobile communication networks--historically implemented as a modular cascade of pilot-aided channel estimation (CE), forward error correction (FEC), cyclic redundancy check (CRC), and hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ)--remain foundational to 5G New Radio (NR). Although finite-blocklength coding, joint estimation-decoding, and grant-free access have been active academic topics for over a decade, commercial 3GPP specifications up to Release 18 still enforce rigid cross-layer boundaries between these blocks. In short-packet machine-type communications (MTC) for IMT-2030 (6G), inserting separate redundancy for channel training, error correction, and error detection shrinks the net payload entropy resolved per channel slot, while standardized UE processing timelines and HARQ round-trip delays collide with sub-millisecond reliability targets. Combining a multi-user MIMO short-packet simulation with real 3GPP TS 38.214 numerology latency budgets, this article diagnoses the structural bottlenecks of the legacy reliability pipeline and outlines an interoperable roadmap for 3GPP Release 20+--spanning soft-output universal decoding, sensing-assisted priors, grant-free joint detection, and task-oriented error control.

papers.title: Sharp Asymptotic Theory of Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Gaussian Processes with a Matern Kernel
papers.abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a flexible framework for modeling complex dependence structures through a covariance function, or kernel, whose parameters determine the variability, correlation, and smoothness of the underlying process. The Matérn kernel is among the most popular choices due to its flexibility in modeling different degrees of smoothness. Although the identifiability of Matérn kernel parameters under fixed-domain asymptotics is completely understood, identifiability alone does not establish the consistency or asymptotic behavior of the maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) routinely used in practice. In this paper, we address this gap by developing a sharp asymptotic theory for the joint MLE of Matérn kernel parameters. Since parameter identifiability depends critically on the dimension of the observation domain, we characterize the estimable parameters and establish their convergence rates across different dimensions. We establish joint asymptotic normality and minimax optimality of the convergence rates. In addition, we establish asymptotically valid confidence regions for the estimable parameters. Our results accommodate irregular sampling designs and extend to sub-Gaussian measurement errors. Extensive simulation studies illustrate the theoretical results.

papers.title: The Coupled Scaled Dirichlet Distribution
papers.abstract: We introduce a coupled scaled Dirichlet distribution for paired compositions that may have different dimensions. Building on the matched Gamma-sharing construction of Trick, Rothkopf, and Jäkel (2023) for ordinary Dirichlet vectors, we allow scaled Dirichlet margins and extend the construction to include crossed sharing between non-corresponding latent components. We propose a signed coupling parameter whose sign selects matched or crossed sharing and whose magnitude controls the strength of sharing. We then develop a time-varying extension in which observed covariates determine this parameter. The model can therefore switch between matched and crossed sharing over time while preserving both scaled Dirichlet margins. We derive the joint mixed moments and use them to estimate dependence after fitting the margins separately. The moments can be evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation or by two-dimensional numerical quadrature, regardless of the dimensions of the compositions. Simulations show that the estimator generally recovers the sharing pattern, although weak crossed sharing is harder to detect. In an application to four U.S. equity-index futures, the time-varying model modestly improved the held-out energy and variogram scores for the trading-volume and intraday price-range compositions relative to the static-dependence model.

papers.title: Dynamics Forcing: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Causal Video World Models
papers.abstract: Causal video world models generate block by block from their own previous outputs. Small errors in early blocks are fed back as history and grow until the scene and the robot fall apart. Teacher forcing trains on clean ground-truth history, so the model never sees the history it will actually condition on, and it also finds a shortcut: copying the previous frame instead of predicting how the scene changes. We present Dynamics Forcing, a training scheme that keeps real video as the only supervision and reshapes how history is presented. History is perturbed in three ways: random noising, self-resampling by the model itself, and joint denoising, in which the most recent blocks are still partly noisy when the next block is predicted. On top of this we move history guidance and first-frame anchor guidance from inference into training, so that the model is pushed to use its history and its reference frame rather than ignore them. Dynamics Forcing needs no teacher model, no distillation, and no additional model at inference. Applied to a 5B video model with LoRA on 77 hours of manipulation video on a single GPU, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.

papers.title: Continuous-time 4D Reconstruction via Event-guided Latent Feature Interpolation
papers.abstract: Recent geometric foundation models can successfully convert a video sequence into frames of registered point clouds, but cannot predict moments beyond the observed temporal resolution. We propose a continuous-time 4D reconstruction method that extracts 3D structure and camera poses at any time instant, with additional guidance from event-camera measurements. While event cameras provide evidence at microsecond resolution to continuously fill the temporal gap, integrating them into existing RGB-based foundation models remains challenging. We formulate the problem as interpolation in the latent feature space and augment event-based losses in the image space as an auxiliary task to boost accuracy. Operating in the latent space leverages the powerful geometric priors of foundation models, while the event loss provides physically grounded guidance. To effectively address the lack of paired training data, we further propose a self-supervised training framework that uses pseudo-ground-truth labels of estimated geometry and simulated events generated from high-frame-rate RGB videos. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed pipeline outperforms baselines that temporally interpolate either the input RGB videos or the estimated geometry, and that it generalizes to unseen real-world scenarios. Controlled experiments with synthetic corruptions show that it remains robust under motion-blur and low-light conditions.

papers.title: Cumulants, Partitions, and Generalizations of Pólya's Characterization of the Normal Distribution
papers.abstract: Let $X_1,X_2$ be independent, identically distributed random variables with finite variance. Pólya (1923) proved the celebrated result that if $\sqrt{2}X_1 =^L X_1+X_2$ then $X_1$ is normally distributed. Pólya's theorem has been extended in many ways, e.g., to the case of random coefficients $R_1,R_2$ such that, under certain regularity conditions, if $(R_1^2+R_2^2)^{1/2}X_1 =^L R_1X_1+R_2X_2$, then $X_1$ is normally distributed. In this article, Pólya's theorem is generalized {\it via} the combinatorics of $Π_n$, the set-partitions of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Let $X_j,R_j$, $j=1,\ldots,n$, be mutually independent random variables, where $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are identically distributed. For each $ν\in Π_n$, a random variable $W_ν$ is constructed from $\{X_j,R_j, j=1,\ldots,n\}$ and, subject to regularity conditions, the normality of $X_1$ is deduced from functional equations involving linear combinations of the characteristic functions of the $W_ν$. For $n = 3$, the $W_ν$ are $(R_1^2+R_2^2+R_3^2)^{1/2}X_1$, $(R_1^2+R_2^2)^{1/2}X_1+R_3X_3$, $(R_1^2+R_3^2)^{1/2}X_1+R_2X_2$, $R_1X_1+(R_2^2+R_3^2)^{1/2}X_2$, and $R_1X_1+R_2X_2+R_3X_3$, corresponding to the partitions $123$, $12|3$, $13|2$, $1|23$, and $1|2|3$, respectively. By modifying the regularity conditions, we also obtain characterizations of some contaminated normal distributions. A characterization of the exponential distribution through the minimum of a random sample leads us consider mutually independent random variables $X_j\ge0$, $R_j>0$, $j=1,\ldots,n$, where $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are identically distributed. For each $ν\inΠ_n$ a random variable $\tilde{W}_ν$ is constructed from $\{X_j,R_j, j=1,\ldots,n\}$ and, subject to regularity conditions, the exponentiality of $X_1$ is derived from functional equations based on linear combinations of the survival functions of the $\tilde{W}_ν$, $ν\inΠ_n$.

papers.title: Identifiability of infinite location-scale Gaussian mixtures
papers.abstract: The problem of identifiability of the mixing measure for a location-scale mixture of Gaussian distributions is considered. We give sufficient and necessary conditions on the compact support of the mixing measure on unknown location and scale parameters for which the mixing measure's uniqueness can be guaranteed. This is achieved by an analytic and probabilistic framework that characterizes the null space of the Gaussian mixing operator, a linear mapping that transforms a space of mixing measures with compact support into that of Gaussian mixture distributions. This framework exposes a fruitful connection between the infinite location-scale Gaussian mixtures and the exiting behavior of a space-time backward Brownian motion from a compact domain, as well as the nature of the support of the heat potential associated with such a stochastic process. As a consequence of this theory we obtain complete characterizations of identifiability for several natural classes of location-scale parameter sets in terms of their topological and geometric properties. Our theory also yields canonical and identifiable representations of infinite Gaussian mixtures with mixing support contained within enclosed boundaries.

papers.title: The replication-energy limit of PQG reduced-density-matrix theory from a single-fragment semidefinite program
papers.abstract: Variational two-electron reduced-density-matrix calculations are not size extensive: the energy per fragment can decrease when identical, strictly noninteracting fragments are replicated [M. Nakata and K. Yasuda, Phys. Rev. A 80, 042109 (2009)]. For the $P$, $Q$, and $G$ conditions (PQG) we prove the following. (i) The energy per fragment converges to the minimum of a semidefinite program (SDP) on one fragment. The limit is reached through negative interfragment covariances of order $1/(k-1)$ for $k$ replicas, which cancel the local electron number and spin fluctuations consistently with a global singlet. (ii) The energy per fragment is nonincreasing in the replica count. (iii) It reaches the limit exactly at a finite replica count. (iv) The defect is tied to the local electron-number variance: a sharp local electron number restores additivity without a spin constraint. (v) In chains of identical units the energy per unit has a limit that tends to the same minimum as the coupling vanishes. The key tool is that the $G$ condition [C. Garrod and J. K. Percus, J. Math. Phys. 5, 1756 (1964)] keeps the variances and covariances of one-body operators positive semidefinite without a representing state, so that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applies. PQG therefore admits explicitly constructed replicated points whose compensated local fluctuations lower the energy per fragment below the isolated value. Be, CH$_4$, N$_2$, and H$_2$O (STO-6G) and a four-site Hubbard fragment illustrate the results; in these examples the gap to the isolated value persists with three-index conditions $T_1$ and $T_2$.

papers.title: Data-Quality-Aware Fundus Classification with Anatomy-Guided Glaucoma Assessment and Cross-Dataset Evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: Deep learning fundus classifiers often perform well internally, but duplicated images, inconsistent labels, acquisition differences and poor threshold transfer can undermine their reliability. We assess nine-class classifiers beyond internal accuracy, using a data audit, frozen-model external evaluation and an anatomy-guided specialist. Methods: Nine-class experts (ConvNeXt-Small, EfficientNetV2-Small, DenseNet169) were trained with three seeds. Auditing 5,318 images for exact duplicates and cross-label conflicts removed 464 conflict groups (942 images) and six same-label copies, leaving 4,370 images. An anatomy-guided glaucoma specialist read disc-centred crops with vessel and disc/cup segmentation maps, plus cup-to-disc features. Frozen models were evaluated on RFMiD and JSIEC, and a prespecified comparison on REFUGE was replicated on ORIGA, G1020 and PAPILA. Results: ConvNeXt-Small reached an internal accuracy of 0.910, macro-F1 of 0.917 and AUC of 0.982; disc and cup Dice scores were 0.966 and 0.915. Across seeds, the fixed anatomy-guided mix left internal accuracy unchanged relative to equal soft voting (-0.001) but raised mean external closed-set accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on RFMiD (positive in two of three seeds) and 2.3 on JSIEC. On REFUGE (800 photographs) it improved balanced accuracy by 7.4 percentage points (95% CI 5.1 to 9.5), and by 2.1 on ORIGA, with positive gains on G1020 and PAPILA. Thresholds transferred poorly (REFUGE sensitivity 0.950, specificity 0.411). Conclusions: Retinal classifiers should be judged by data-quality auditing, anatomy-informed modelling and multi-cohort evaluation. Anatomy-guided fusion improved transfer at no internal cost, but gains varied by cohort and thresholds did not transfer, so internal metrics alone do not establish reliable performance.

papers.title: Computational Strategies for Mixed Logit Estimation Automatic Differentiation, GPU Computing, and Floating-Point Precision
authors: Hengzhe Zhao Jinhui Zhang Yuanyuan Gu
papers.abstract: Mixed logit estimation can become computationally demanding as sample size and the dimension of preference heterogeneity increase. This study examines how derivative computation, processor choice and floating-point precision affect estimation time and parameter recovery across problem sizes. This paper provides a controlled benchmark, comparing finite differences (FD) with automatic differentiation (AD), central processing unit (CPU) execution with graphics processing unit (GPU) execution, and double-precision (FP64) with single-precision (FP32) arithmetic using Monte Carlo experiments that hold the data-generating process, simulation draws, optimiser, starting values, and objective function fixed across strategies. The results show that AD is the dominant source of acceleration. Combining AD with FP32 arithmetic provides further gains, while combining AD, GPU execution, and FP32 arithmetic delivers the largest speed improvements, particularly as sample size and model complexity increase. Our findings indicate substantial computational gains with broadly comparable parameter-recovery performance in the simulated settings considered.An empirical application in health preferences illustrates what extra empirical evidence and statistical benefit on model fit could be achieved, when researchers are made possible to estimate a richer, correlated preference specification. We provide an open sourced prototype to for model estimation with AD-FP32 strategy workflow that automatically detect hardware and provide the fastest estimation. Faster estimation can make richer random-coefficient specifications, larger simulation draw counts, bootstrap inference, multi-start optimisation, and robustness checks more feasible in applied choice modelling research.

papers.title: Higher Realizability Toposes
papers.abstract: Building on $\infty$-tripos theory, we develop a theory of realizability $\infty$-toposes. We apply $\infty$-tripos theory to construct the function, modified, and Krivine realizability $\infty$-toposes. We recover the Lawvere-Tierney nucleus $j$ that specifies local truth in each construction by exhibiting, for any $n\geq1$, a single family of Eilenberg-MacLane $n$-types whose fibre at an ambient truth value $p$ is contractible after sheafification precisely when $j(p)$ holds. In function realizability, we relate identity types to descriptive set theory. For each $n\geq 2$, we construct a univalent classifier $U_n$ of exact truncation height $n+1$. As maps from Baire space into $U_n$ vary, the sets of inputs admitting a global path from the assigned code to the terminal code are exactly the $G_δ$ subsets of Baire space. After exponentiation by Baire space, the analogous test against the constant map at the terminal code yields exactly the coanalytic sets, at the same truncation height. In modified realizability, a closed proof of local existence under a stable numerical precondition yields a total recursive function together with a coherent proof that its output satisfies the specification whenever the precondition holds. In Krivine realizability, contextual choice for $(n-1)$-truncated families over suitable $n$-types recovers the subterminal defining the Boolean localization. Binary cohomology distinguishes slices of Anel-Awodey-Barton's effective $\infty$-topos even when they share the same ordinary Hyland effective topos and their bases have equivalent spaces of global points. Hyland's effective topos thus occurs as the category of zero-types in infinitely many pairwise inequivalent realizability $\infty$-toposes (recovering Hyland's effective topos as the category of zero-types does not uniquely determine an effective $\infty$-topos).

papers.title: Baker-Akhiezer realization and reconstruction for three-wave interactions in canonical multiwave Hamiltonian
papers.abstract: We revisit the canonical multiwave Hamiltonians with three-wave interactions studied by Menyuk, Chen and Lee, and by Jiang, Rauch-Wojciechowski and Bullough. With compatible linear phase terms, we construct their general solution on the generic spectral locus from multipoint Baker-Akhiezer functions. Conversely, we give a finite interpolation criterion and completion procedure that realize prescribed Baker-Akhiezer evaluations on arbitrary smooth algebraic curves in the same Hamiltonian system. We identify the prescribed curve with the normalized spectral curve and show that commuting polynomial Hamiltonians span every Abel direction on each birational spectral level, including the accompanying mode phases. Together, these results establish a correspondence between Baker-Akhiezer data and canonical multiwave dynamics, supporting our view of this system as a fundamental canonical Hamiltonian setting for Baker-Akhiezer functions. We make explicit its connections with other established integrable systems and validate hyperelliptic, trigonal and multipuncture examples numerically.

papers.title: Higher Duality Theory: Geometric HoTT and Classifying $\infty$-Toposes
papers.abstract: We develop geometric homotopy type theory (geometric HoTT), which gives a dependent language for constructions preserved by inverse images of geometric morphisms. We give a homotopy-coherent calculus for geometric HoTT and extend the classical duality between geometric logic and classifying toposes to Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes. For each geometric type theory, the $\infty$-category of contexts generated by its rules is equivalent to its classifying $\infty$-topos. As the theory varies, the classifier gives a duality of $(\infty,2)$-categories between geometric HoTT theories with interpretations and Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes with geometric morphisms. We then construct a universal family of classifying $\infty$-toposes whose fiber at each presentation of a theory is the classifying $\infty$-topos of that theory. We also construct a universal family of classifying $\infty$-toposes with coherent transport along Morita equivalences of theories. Geometric HoTT thus serves as an internal language for Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes, extending the role of geometric logic in classical topos theory to the realm of $\infty$-topos theory.

papers.title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring
papers.abstract: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.

papers.title: The Complexity of Full-Information Iterated Protocols
papers.abstract: Full-information protocols are a common abstraction in distributed computing. In its iterated form, processes proceed through successive communication rounds in which each process shares its entire current knowledge of the execution. Usually, it is implicitly assumed that a process can transmit an unbounded amount of information in every round. This paper makes that assumption explicit and studies its computational cost. We formalize the problem of simulating iterated full-information protocols when communication is bounded, so that each process may share at most $b$ bits with every other process per round. We show that for a large family of shared-memory communication models and $n+1$ processes, simulating $r$ iterations of the full-information protocol requires \(Ω\!\left((n!)^{r-1} 2^{\,n-b}\right)\) rounds. We complement this lower bound with simulation algorithms that are asymptotically optimal in the conventional read-write model. In particular, the case of two processes is special: $r$ iterations of a full-information protocol can be simulated in exactly $r$ rounds while using only $2$-bit variables, as the amount of information that must be represented remains bounded for two processes but grows with each iteration for $n \geq 2$.

papers.title: Modulation equations and coherence dynamics in a qubit chain coupled to a circulating fluxon
papers.abstract: We derive modulation equations for the joint quantum amplitudes of a circulating fluxon and an exchange-coupled qubit chain whose endpoint interacts with the field. A unitary passage operator combines the translational packet, vacuum dressing, and discrete oscillatory modes. A resonant normal form separates the slow amplitude evolution from nonresonant corrections. Ordered emission and return amplitudes generate a second-order correction that changes the population and coherence of an internal qubit. The next ground-band coefficient gives compensating diagonal and near-resonant off-diagonal contributions to the accumulated error. We bound the state error a posteriori. At a velocity-selected resonance, direct propagation over 81 passages gives a mode contribution of order $6\times10^{-8}$; the cubic ground-band approximation agrees with an expanded full calculation to $1.5\times10^{-9}$ in the tested observables. The equations describe how the source profile and field memory affect coherence inside the chain.

papers.title: Essentially Order-Preserving Fourth-Order Exponential Runge--Kutta Methods for Non-Commuting Operators
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the convergence of explicit exponential Runge--Kutta methods for the linear evolution equation \(u'(t)+Au(t)=Bu(t)\), where \(-A\) generates an analytic semigroup, \(B\) is unbounded and relatively bounded with respect to \(A\), and \(A\) and \(B\) do not commute. It is known from our previous work on order reduction of exponential Runge--Kutta methods for non-commuting operators that this non-commutativity can cause order reduction even for linear problems. In a further work on third-order methods, we showed that this reduction can be avoided by adding a stage and imposing higher regularity on the initial data. Here we treat the fourth-order case. We identify conditions on the coefficients of explicit fourth-order exponential Runge--Kutta methods under which the full order four is retained for this class of problems, and we state the convergence rate as a function of the regularity of \(u_0\). The analysis shows precisely which defect terms, caused by the non-commutativity of \(A\) and \(B\), are eliminated by these conditions. The classical methods of Krogstad and of Strehmel--Weiner do not satisfy them and converge only with order \(11/4\) under the corresponding regularity assumptions, whereas the six-stage method expRK4s6, constructed by Luan (2021), satisfies them and attains order four. Numerical experiments for an advection--diffusion problem involving non-commuting operators confirm the theoretical convergence rates.

papers.title: Twisted K-Theory and Reduced Norms over Global and Higher Local Fields
papers.abstract: We prove the Merkurjev--Suslin conjecture concerning reduced norms over both global and local fields. Furthermore, in both settings, we construct maps between truncated K-theory spectra that induce the reduced norms in degrees 1 and 2, and show that these maps are equivalences over local fields. Over global fields, we establish finiteness properties of their fibers and give a detailed description of their structure. We also extend the Merkurjev--Suslin conjecture to two-dimensional local fields and three-dimensional local fields with characteristic sequences (0, 0, 0) and (0, 0, p), and prove it in these settings. Finally, we apply these results to noncommutative class field theory over number fields and obtain a description of the Artin map associated with a central simple algebra.

papers.title: Memphis: A Case Study in Seeding an Agent Task from a Model's Real-World Attempt
papers.abstract: Agent benchmarks are usually made harder by scaling up the data their tasks are built from, yet models that do well on them still fail at real work. We propose building simulated tasks from a model's own attempt at an open-ended task in the real world, so that the model's failures in the simulation resemble its failures in reality. As a case study, we had GPT-6.1 Sol manage two human workers in Cairo over chat for five shifts, with a budget of 7,000 Egyptian pounds, to build as many USB desk lamps as it could. It built two. From the real-world attempt's transcript, we build Memphis, an evaluation in a model-simulated world. Memphis is hard: GPT-6.1 Sol delivers 1.0 lamp per trial on average and repeats its real-world mistakes, buying too few stands and giving up the search for them. With a one-page hint on where to buy parts and who can wire them, it delivers 9.2. Claude Opus 5.5 delivers 2.2 without the hint and 4.6 with it. We release the task, the trials, the audits, and a redacted record of the real-world evaluation.

papers.title: Compactification and non-zero density in (2+1)-dimensional four-fermion model
papers.abstract: The phase diagram of (2+1)-dimensional NJL type model has been studied with one compact dimension. The effect of compactification and fermion density on the chiral symmetry breaking is considered for periodic boundary conditions.

papers.title: Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their output. We generated 90 websites for three projects using combinations of three coding agents, four language models, and multiple reasoning-effort levels. We evaluated complete interaction journeys using axe-core, IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, and QualWeb, and converged reports to observe violation prevalence and violated WCAG Success Criterion (SC). None of the 90 baseline websites was fully accessible, with an average of 80.43 violated interface elements. 13 WCAG SCs were violated at least once across the runs. Color contrast was the most prevalent issue, followed by labeling, semantic-structure, keyboard, and visualization failures. We reran 24 matched configurations with a general accessibility Skill and a contrast-specific Skill. Both significantly improved accessibility scores, but neither eliminated violations. User testing with blind individuals corroborated the experiential effects of the detected inaccessibilities. Moreover, functional correctness decreased with the inclusion of Skills. Our findings show that accessibility does not reliably emerge from vibe coding, and agentic interventions can both improve some accessibility issues and introduce new functional ones.

papers.title: A linear bound in Waring's problem
papers.abstract: We show that $G(k) \asymp k$ in Waring's problem.

papers.title: Extreme Value Theory for Peak Power in Discrete-Time Complex Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: The peak power for a band-limited, radio frequency (RF) signal, often expressed using the dimensionless peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR), is an important quantity for signal analysis and the design of RF transmitters and receivers. Modern digital instrumentation, like vector signal analyzers, collect and process discrete-time samples of the complex baseband signal. Also, computer-based simulations of continuous-time processes must be carried out with discrete-time sequences. Therefore, to design such measurements and simulations, accurate models for the distribution of the PAPR for discrete-time complex baseband processes are required. In particular, band-pass thermal noise and modern communication signals, like orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), are often modeled as complex Gaussian processes. To address this problem, we present a new analytical model for the PAPR distribution of a stationary, discrete-time, complex Gaussian process. We demonstrate that the new discrete-time model subsumes prior models based on asymptotic extreme value theory as special cases while providing a larger domain of efficacy. Specifically, using Monte Carlo simulations of filtered complex white Gaussian noise, we show that the new model is more effective for practical sample sizes and dual-band spectra than previous approaches.

papers.title: General bounds for metric dimension of diameter-two graphs with applications
papers.abstract: We study the metric dimension of several classes of graphs with diameter two. First, we establish a general lower bound for the metric dimension of graphs with diameter two in terms of their order and maximum degree. We then apply our results to Grassmann graphs, Moore graphs, and bilinear forms graphs. For Kneser graphs, we obtain new upper bounds, while for $G_q(n,2)$ Grassmann graphs we establish new upper bounds provided by constructions of resolving sets. For Moore graphs of diameter two, we derive improved lower bounds, and for $H_q(n,2)$ bilinear forms graphs, we obtain new upper and lower bounds on their metric dimension.

papers.title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?
papers.abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.

papers.title: Mixed-State Magnetotransport Below $T_c$ in Type-II Superconducting NbN Thin Films
papers.abstract: The transport properties of type-II superconductors in the mixed state below the superconducting transition temperature, $T_c$, remain difficult to interpret because superconducting and dissipative processes coexist in the presence of a magnetic field. To investigate this regime in NbN thin films, we measured the field-dependent sheet resistance ($R^M_{xx}$) and Hall resistance ($R^M_{xy}$) below $T_c$ in Van der Pauw geometry for 4-nm-thick NbN films on sapphire and silicon substrates at driving currents of 1 mA and 2 mA. By combining the longitudinal response with the antisymmetrized Hall signal, we use a phenomenological current-partition model to estimate the dissipative and superconducting current contributions. From this analysis, we estimate the field-dependent superconducting current together with the Hall-derived effective dissipative carrier density and mobility. We also observe an even-in-field transverse signal whose magnitude depends strongly on the driving current. We discuss this signal as a possible mixed-state response involving the magnetic and supercurrent texture of Abrikosov vortices, vortex dynamics, and Cooper-pair current redistribution. The present measurements do not uniquely distinguish vortex, condensate, or combined contributions. The model provides a practical way to compare the longitudinal and transverse mixed-state responses without implying a direct spatial separation of the two current channels.

papers.title: Predicting the Orbital Retention of Habitable-Zone Planets Following Stellar Flybys Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Stellar flybys can significantly alter the orbital configurations of planetary systems, potentially displacing planets initially located within the habitable zone (HZ) of their host stars. In this study, we investigate the dynamical effects of stellar encounters on HZ planets using a large suite of three-body N-body simulations. We examine how the properties of the host star, passing star, planetary orbit, and encounter geometry influence the final orbital configuration. A planet is considered to retain an HZ orbit only if it remains bound to its original host and its entire final orbital range, from periastron to apastron, lies within the HZ boundaries. Based on the simulation results, we develop an XGBoost classifier to predict the final HZ status of planets following stellar encounters. The model achieves an accuracy of 0.90, an ROC-AUC of 0.97, and a PR-AUC of 0.97 on the test set. Feature importance analysis identifies the encounter-impulse parameter as the dominant predictor of the outcome. The classifier provides a computational speedup of approximately 74 compared with direct N-body simulations. We further evaluate the model using an independent dataset representing a globular-cluster environment, where approximately 20 per cent of planets retain HZ orbits. Despite the naturally imbalanced class distribution, the model achieves an accuracy of 0.87, an ROC-AUC of 0.92, and a PR-AUC of 0.77. These results demonstrate the potential of machine learning for efficiently predicting the dynamical retention of HZ planets following stellar encounters and for investigating their outcomes in dense stellar environments.

papers.title: Model Immunization Cannot Reliably Protect Models from Harmful Adaptation
papers.abstract: Efficient fine-tuning techniques have substantially reduced the cost of adapting open-weight models, enabling malicious actors to readily fine-tune them toward harmful capabilities. In response, model immunization modifies a pretrained checkpoint to resist subsequent adaptation toward designated harmful capabilities while preserving its utility and adaptability for benign tasks. Furthermore, a few immunization methods have sought to keep their protection robust to some changes in the attacker's adaptation. However, fine-tuning offers attackers many more low-cost options, and we observe that existing methods still substantially overfit to the attacker configuration they are optimized against. Such overfitting stays hidden when immunization is evaluated under, or near, this configuration, so the reported protection may give a false sense of security. To rigorously evaluate model immunization, we conduct experiments, varying one component of this configuration at a time: the harmful data, the adaptation strategy, or the model initialization. Across four immunization methods on text-to-image generation and image classification, with additional results on language models, these variations substantially degrade the protection, and in many cases the immunized model relearns the harmful capability nearly as well as the un-immunized model. Existing immunization therefore cannot reliably protect models, leaving them vulnerable to harmful adaptation.

papers.title: Inferring Experimental Objectives in Microscopy Experiments from Decision Traces
papers.abstract: Modern microscopes can acquire, analyze and act on data far faster than human operators can decide what to measure next. Exploiting this speed in automated experiments requires the instrument to follow the scientific logic of the operator, and one way to encode that logic is through reward functions that become part of the operation process. Here we explore whether such reward functions can be learned from the decision histories of microscope operators. We propose multiple frameworks in which recorded choices among alternative measurement locations serve as comparative evidence about the operator's preferences, and we compare several algorithms for reconstructing the reward including interpretable linear models built on physically meaningful image descriptors, nonlinear functions of the same descriptors, an unsupervised image representation followed by preference modeling, and a preference trained deep kernel inspired model. The result of this analysis is a spatial field of reward functions over the sample that can be used to run the instrument. We also propose a way to benchmark these approaches, based on withheld decisions and on decision histories generated with known objectives. We then examine the possibility that a decision history contains changing priorities throughout the experiment. A hidden Markov model assigns distinct rewards to recurring selection strategies, whereas a continuous-state model tracks smoothly varying preference weights. Controlled sequences generated over real microscopy candidate sets show that both concealed switches and gradual drift can be recovered. These reward functions, learned directly from recorded decisions, provide candidate objectives for future automated microscopy experiments.

papers.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head for Tiny Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.

papers.title: Form of Words in Free Products with scl 1/12
papers.abstract: Let $G = *_λG_λ$ be a free product of groups and let $g\in G$ be any element not conjugate into any free factor and not conjugate to its inverse. Then $\mathrm{scl}(g) \ge \frac{1}{12}$ and $\mathrm{scl}(g) = \frac{1}{12}$ if and only if $g$ is a product of an element of order $2$ and an element of order $3$. In particular, this classifies all elements in $G = \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{Z})$ with $\mathrm{scl}_G(g) = \frac{1}{12}$.
