papers.abstract: The evolving cellular networks continue to rely on the legacy GPRS Tunneling Protocol-User Plane (GTP-U) to encapsulate and route user data traffic across the data plane. Recent security research demonstrated that nested GTP-U (GTP-in-GTP) payload vulnerabilities enable a diverse range of attacks on victim users. To address this vulnerability, in this paper, we propose a closed-loop extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and eXpress Data Path (XDP) defense to detect and mitigate nested GTP-U attacks in 5G and beyond networks. The proposed framework contains three components: an in-kernel XDP Detection and Drop Module (XDP-DDM), a user-space User-Plane Telemetry Agent (UP-TA), and a multi-threaded Control-Plane Mitigation Orchestrator (CP-MO). We implement and evaluate the proposed defense on a sliced 5G testbed integrating Free5GC, UERANSIM, and Containerlab. Experimental results indicate that the XDP-DDM detects and drops malicious nested GTP-U packets at line rate, while the UP-TA and CP-MO asynchronously report and revoke the attacker's network access, respectively. Under a 10,000 packets-per-second cross-slice nested GTP-U flood, the proposed solution preserves the baseline performance of the victim slices while introducing minimal overhead. We also show that the proposed solution has minimal impact on the user's throughput and round-trip time.

papers.title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation
papers.abstract: Blind quantum computation lets a client delegate a computation while hiding it from the server, up to a declared leakage. Its security definitions cover a single round. A variational quantum algorithm, however, delegates many rounds, and its classical optimizer decides from private data when to stop. We study what the resulting round count tells an honest-but-curious server. For protocols with one-time-padded transcripts and fresh randomness in every round, we prove that the server's best distinguishing advantage over the whole sequence equals the total-variation distance between the stopping-time distributions, so the round count is the only residual channel in this model. We also show that soundness composes as $δ\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ under adaptive stopping, given a conditional per-round soundness property that composably secure verifiable protocols provide. In simulated delegated eigensolvers for the transverse-field Ising chain, the local Polyak-Lojasiewicz ratio measured in iterations 5 to 15 predicts the noiseless stopping round with a leave-one-out error of 1.7 iterations, compared with 10.3 for a constant predictor. Across 14 configurations that differ in optimizer, stopping rule, initialization, system size, shot budget and problem family, the leakage is significant in 12 and ranges from 0.14 to 1.68 bits, and a maximum-entropy bound estimated on held-out sessions lies above it in all of them. For defense, we show that any mechanism acting after the stopping decision can only add rounds, and that differentially private padding costs the full adjacency radius. A fixed public iteration budget removes the channel completely; set at the median run length, it costs 10% of the remaining energy gap. A differentially private stopping rule based on AboveThreshold protects every pair of instances, but it must often stop too early, which makes it costly.

papers.title: Exact many-body scars of generic spin models from singlet covers
papers.abstract: The square-lattice transverse-field Ising model has exact zero-energy eigenstates at any field: products of singlets on alternate plaquette diagonals. A longitudinal field isolates them from a symmetry-protected degeneracy. The mechanism is that a site coupled equally to both ends of a singlet annihilates it. The result thus holds for any spin $s$, anisotropic exchange, a large class of bond disorder and certain three-spin terms. This mechanism decides which lattices host such states: two of the 11 Archimedean lattices (four at $s=1/2$), bcc and quasicrystals with spins on the edges. Singlet pumping cools any state into them.

papers.title: DREAM: Dual-Memory Reasoning for Anticipatory 3D Perception in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving systems must not only interpret the current scene but also anticipate perceptual challenges such as occlusions, sparse observations, and recurring failure patterns. However, most existing LiDAR semantic segmentation methods operate in a frame-centric manner, processing each scan independently and discarding past contextual experience, which limits robustness under dynamic scene changes. We propose DREAM, a Dual-memory REAsoning framework for continual LiDAR seMantic segmentation that reframes perception as an experience-driven and anticipatory process. DREAM maintains two complementary memory banks in a strictly online setting: a latent memory that stores compact semantic abstractions of previously observed scenes, and an error memory that records representations associated with uncertain predictions. At each timestep, relevant memory entries are retrieved via cosine similarity and integrated into the feature space through a lightweight modulation mechanism, enabling the model to reinforce consistent semantic patterns while suppressing recurring failure modes. The backbone remains frozen and no past scans are replayed, ensuring computational efficiency and bounded memory growth. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks demonstrate that DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with consistent improvements on dynamic and small-scale objects, highlighting the effectiveness of persistent and error-aware memory for robust long-horizon perception.

papers.title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. We find that more units die as the layer's inputs lie farther from zero relative to how much they vary. We call this ratio the offset. Earlier work showed this in sparse autoencoders at the start of training. We saw it after training in agents, image classifiers, a reservoir computer and sparse autoencoders on GPT-2. A random encoder leaves the offset of its input roughly unchanged, and a formula predicted its median offset within 25 percent in all 44 cases. So a game with a bright, mostly unchanging screen gives the next layer a large offset. In Pong, subtracting the average screen raised the number of live units from between 3 and 6 of 64 to between 59 and 63, so the number alone cannot show a game's complexity. On unaltered screens none of the agents reached a training score of 18 in 50 million steps. With the subtraction all did within 5 million, about as fast as a trained encoder on unaltered screens. In Breakout the subtraction left more units alive, but average training scores did not clearly improve, and a large gap to a trained encoder remained. So we do not treat their number as something to raise for its own sake. The evidence is from small networks and three games, and in agents and image classifiers changing the offset also changed the size of the inputs. We suggest measuring the offset before training a layer on a fixed front end and, if it is large, trying to subtract the mean input.

papers.title: A compact nonformal manifold with holonomy Spin(7)
papers.abstract: We construct a compact simply connected eight-manifold with holonomy Spin(7) and a triple Massey product of degrees $(3,2,2)$ that does not contain zero. The manifold is a resolution of a flat orbifold. Joyce's gluing theorem gives it a torsion-free Spin(7) structure. The resolution map factors through a quotient of $Y\times S^1$, where $Y$ is Martín-Merchán's nonformal $G_2$ manifold. The map to this quotient has degree one, so pullback preserves a nonzero Massey pairing. On the resolution the detecting degree-two class annihilates the full indeterminacy. Simple connectivity and nonformality imply full Spin(7) holonomy. The manifold has $(b_2,b_3,b_4^+,b_4^-)=(22,10,91,27)$.

papers.title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
papers.abstract: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.

papers.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.

papers.title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
papers.abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.

papers.title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.

papers.title: The probability that two random generalized derangements have the same number of cycles
papers.abstract: Using singularity analysis, we show that the probability that two independently and uniformly selected generalized derangements of size $n$ have the same number of cycles is asymptotically the same as the corresponding probability for unrestricted permutations, namely, $\sim \frac{1}{2\sqrt{π\log n}}\;.$

papers.title: Agentic Root Cause Reasoning and Localization of Unsoundness in Static Call Graph Analysis
papers.abstract: Static call graph tools cannot soundly model every dynamic language feature, yet rarely reveal when, where, or why their results are unsound. We present CGRizz, an agentic framework that diagnoses unsoundness for developers and warns users about it. During training, CGRizz compares static and dynamic call graphs to identify boundary edges: calls observed at runtime but missing from the static graph. For each edge, an LLM agent proposes a root cause, including the unmodeled program pattern and responsible tool location. CGRizz validates each proposal using three independent forms of evidence: runtime instrumentation detecting the pattern, a test case reproducing the missing edge, and a warning inserted at the implicated tool location. Validated reports help developers diagnose limitations, while the warnings form an instrumented build that flags potential unsoundness in new programs without dynamic analysis. We evaluate CGRizz on three benchmark suites using WALA, OPAL, and Soot. Of 1,459 boundary edges, CGRizz reasons about 10.3% directly, all confirmed by manual audit, and resolves another 84.1% by grouping edges with validated root causes. Tool maintainers confirmed several limitations, some of which have been fixed. The warnings flag 74%-92% of unsoundness in held-out programs. Guided by CGRizz reports, a coding agent refactored programs to remove 64% of targeted root-cause patterns while preserving functionality.

papers.title: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
papers.abstract: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. In both, a label is assigned according to the entity that sends the funds. We ask whether models trained on these benchmarks learn how laundering moves or merely who sent the money, and we propose a diagnostic protocol to tell the two apart: a sender lookup baseline, a novelty baseline, a sender-disjoint split with a leakage check, and a decomposition of performance into sender, receiver and intrinsic signal. On Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender. Under the standard random split, a no-learning lookup of sender history reaches a PR-AUC of 0.954, against 0.975 for gradient boosting on 456 features; our reimplementation of RevClassify reproduces its reported 0.97 and falls to 0.126 without sender information. When senders are held out, performance drops to 0.746, and the subgraph's own structure, transactions and receivers fall from 0.619 to 0.186. On Elliptic++ the same protocol finds the shortcut negligible: sender history reaches only 0.340 against 0.986 for the full model (3.5 against 10.1 times the test prevalence), adding it to the full model raises PR-AUC by less than 0.004 in every seed, and the transaction's own features keep 0.883 when sending addresses are held out. We trace the difference to the unit of sender identity: Elliptic2 senders are entity clusters that recur across many labeled subgraphs, whereas Elliptic++ senders are individual addresses, and fewer than half of test transactions have a sending address seen in training. A shared sender-based label rule thus produces a severe shortcut in one benchmark and a negligible one in the other, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

papers.title: On the linear stability of elliptic relative equilibrium in planar restricted $(n+1)$-body problem
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider the restricted $(n+1)$-body problems, where the $n$ primaries forming an a homographic motion generated by the planar central configuration, and the massless particle is attracted by this $n$ primaries. We are interested in the linear stability of the elliptic relative equilibria of the massless particle under the pulsating coordinates. The main contribution of this paper first lies in the investigation of a general $(α,β)$-system (1.7). We obtain large-range spectral instability and small-range stability results valid for arbitrary eccentricity. The restricted $(n+1)$-body problem arises as a special case of this system. Accordingly, we derive several criteria for spectral instability and linear stability for this problem. As a final application, we establish some stability results of elliptic relative equilibria for massless particle under some special central configurations.

papers.title: Giant magnetic anisotropy in layered polar metal Sr$_3$Co$_2$O$_7$ from Charge-disproportionation orbital unquenching
papers.abstract: Crystal-field quenching usually suppresses orbital angular momentum and limits magnetic anisotropy in transition-metal oxides. Here we identify charge disproportionation as a route to giant magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the layered polar metal Sr$_3$Co$_2$O$_7$. First-principles calculations reveal an energy preference of 234.0 meV per cell for in-plane [110] magnetization over [001]. Charge disproportionation and the associated polar displacement reconstruct the local cobalt crystal fields, creating inequivalent sites with distinct orbital hierarchies. This reconstruction enables a strongly directional orbital response, particularly at the displaced cobalt site, where orbital angular momentum is recovered for in-plane magnetization. Spin--orbit coupling converts this response into a large magnetic anisotropic energy. In the centrosymmetric reference, the orbital moments remain nearly quenched and the anisotropy is strongly reduced. A local Green-function and orbital-moment analysis connects the large energy scale to orbital unquenching, while the conventional second-order contribution is small within the adopted approximation. These results identify charge-disproportionation-driven orbital reconstruction as a design principle for large anisotropy and motivate layered perovskites and magnetic polar metals as platforms in the search for rare-earth-free permanent magnets.

papers.title: MISeg-Agent: A Human-in-the-Loop Agentic Framework for Error Diagnosis and Executable Prompt Review in 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Despite the strong performance of modern medical image segmentation models, their predictions can still contain localized errors that compromise segmentation quality. Identifying and correcting these errors is therefore essential for improving the reliability of existing segmentation results. While interactive segmentation models enable targeted corrections, identifying potential errors, determining where to intervene, and evaluating corrective actions remain challenging. Moreover, each correction changes the current mask, requiring subsequent error diagnosis and recommendations to adapt accordingly. To address these challenges, we propose MISeg-Agent, a human-in-the-loop agentic framework that diagnoses segmentation errors and provides evidence-based correction recommendations. MISeg-Agent first selects a suitable pretrained segmentation model based on benchmark performance and computational requirements. Given its predicted mask, the framework identifies potential missing and excess foreground regions and recommends suspicious slices and corrective points for review. The framework then evaluates candidate point prompts using an interactive segmentation model and presents the resulting corrections for human verification before applying them. By operating directly on images and predicted masks, the error diagnosis process remains independent of the underlying segmentation model architecture. Evaluations on CT datasets demonstrate that MISeg-Agent improves initial segmentation results and produces final masks closely aligned with reference annotations. By integrating adaptive error diagnosis with validated correction recommendations, MISeg-Agent provides an interpretable approach to identifying and reducing residual errors in existing medical image segmentations.

papers.title: Two-term Rogers dilogarithm identities over cubic fields
papers.abstract: We study normalized two-term Rogers dilogarithm relations in cubic fields. For integral, nonunimodular rank-two monomial configurations whose base argument generates a totally real cubic field, finite-prime valuations force the arguments and their complements to be units. Normalization preserves the generated order and reduces the problem to two cubic families without a maximal-order assumption. In the simplest cubic family, an existing unit-equation classification yields exactly ten relations up to simultaneous reflection, with distinct coefficients 2, 3, 7, 13, 19, 31 and 97. Explicit five-term certificates prove all ten evaluations. In the second family, a sharpened lower bound for the height of a solution, together with the two-logarithm theorem of Laurent, Mignotte and Nesterenko, reduces the unit equation to a short certified computation, and the family contributes no relation in this class. A unit-index argument restricts, independently, wedge relations between arbitrary exceptional units of non-Galois totally real cubic fields: any such relation would have a coefficient with no prime factor below 23 and would contradict Ennola's conjecture on fundamental units. In cubic fields with one real embedding, the only five-term certified relation between exceptional units with coefficient greater than one is Lewin's identity. Together, these results give exactly eleven identities in the two classes considered, up to the stated reflections.

papers.title: Turing Completeness of Greedy UNO with an Ultimately Periodic Infinite Deck
papers.abstract: We encode an arbitrary two-counter Minsky machine as a two-player UNO round with an ultimately periodic infinite draw pile $uw^ω$. The construction uses a fixed $17$-card prefix and a period of length quadratic in the number of instructions. When both players follow the same fixed greedy policy, the round terminates exactly when the machine halts, and every available hand play has a unique card type. Consequently, greedy termination and victory by a designated player -- as well as winning-strategy existence under forced-play rules without tie-breaking -- are $Σ^0_1$-complete. Under official voluntary-draw rules with unrestricted legal choices, however, the existence of a finite play is decidable (and primitive recursive) via reachability in fixed-dimension vector addition systems with states (VASS). Finally, the maximal duration of a finite greedy play has no total computable upper bound in the input length.

papers.title: TPTL-dist: A Formalised Calculus with Proof Automation for Verifying Real-Time Distributed Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce TPTL-dist, a temporal logic and labelled sequent calculus for specifying and verifying real-time distributed systems. TPTL-dist is formalised in Agda to provide machine-checked correctness and tool support, including automation through a proof search that runs inside Agda. The logic extends Timed Propositional Temporal Logic (TPTL) with past operators, freeze quantification, comparisons between time expressions, domain-specific atoms, and an induction principle on time. We provide a world-based semantics, develop an interval-annotated calculus, and establish its soundness w.r.t. the semantics. To demonstrate its expressiveness, we encode standard distributed system patterns, and we carry out a mechanised proof of a key real-time property of the Pistis Byzantine broadcast protocol. Our results show that TPTL-dist provides a uniform, mechanised framework for reasoning about temporal properties of distributed systems.

papers.title: Deterministic Proper Positive-Only Learning Is Independent of ZFC
papers.abstract: Binary classification from positive-only samples is a variant of PAC learning in which the learner receives i.i.d. samples only from the positive region of an unknown target concept, but is evaluated on the full distribution. Improper learnability in this model has a textbook characterization, whereas proper learnability has remained open for decades. Recent work characterized it for learners with access to randomness, and showed that, unlike in PAC learning, some classes are properly learnable with randomness but not without it, leaving the deterministic case open. We show that this case cannot be resolved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC): there is a class of VC dimension two whose deterministic proper learnability is independent of ZFC, even though a randomized learner provably learns it. Moreover, no dimension of finite character, a desirable property shared by most dimensions in learning theory, characterizes deterministic proper learnability. We also show that the size of the domain is decisive. In ZFC, deterministic proper learnability has a combinatorial characterization on every domain whose cardinality is below a certain threshold, including every countable domain. In contrast, this characterization fails on every domain of sufficiently large cardinality. Under the generalized continuum hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: it is the exact cardinality at which the characterization starts to fail. Finally, our proofs introduce new tools, based on the Erdos--Rado partition theorem, that may be of broader interest.

papers.title: Superpotentials for F-manifolds and bi-flat F-structures on the orbit spaces of reflection groups
papers.abstract: We extend Dubrovin's construction of a superpotential from Frobenius manifolds to biflat F-manifolds. The key step in this extension is choosing a flat coordinate of one of the connections studied in [11] and invert this coordinate with respect to the spectral parameter and the construction does not require an invariant metric. Suppose that the manifold has dimension n and that the superpotential admits a holomorphic continuation to n simple critical points with distinct critical values. These values give canonical coordinates, and the residue formulas recover both the product and the flat connection from the superpotential alone. Conversely, under suitable nondegeneracy conditions, a solution of the superpotential equations for a given product defines a biflat F-manifold. For $B_n$ and $G(m,1,n)$ we obtain the whole family of biflat structures from a polynomial superpotential by varying a twisted primary differential. For $G(m,m,n)$ we obtain the natural biflat structure from a Laurent superpotential. Keeping the Laurent polynomial fixed and varying the primary differential gives a new family of flat F-manifolds depending on one parameter. We use the superpotential and the poles of the dual product along the reflecting hyperplanes to prove the conjecture we formulated in [8] for irreducible Coxeter groups and in [10] for well generated complex reflection groups. The conjecture concerns biflat F-structures whose dual connection has the form studied by Dunkl and Kohno. When the reflecting hyperplanes form a single orbit, we identify the biflat structure associated with the flat structure of [24,25,27]. We obtain the remaining families from the polynomial construction for $G(m,1,n)$ and an explicit computation for $F_4$. In every case the first flat structure extends polynomially to the whole quotient, and the biflat structure is defined on the complement of the reflection discriminant.

papers.title: Seeing Beyond Names: Image-Grounded Concept Linking for Robust Vision-Language Recognition
papers.abstract: A zero-shot vision-language classifier is highly sensitive to the class names it receives. Even when images remain unchanged, replacing familiar labels with synonyms, abbreviations, or ontology terms can significantly alter predictions. We investigate this \emph{vocabulary shift} using a leakage-free evaluation protocol across Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetV2. With CLIP ViT-B/16, alternative class names reduce top-1 accuracy by $14.8$--$17.6$ percentage points. To address this issue, we propose \emph{image-grounded concept linking}, a training-free method that maps class names to visual concepts and uses a reliability gate to improve predictions. The method outperforms a template ensemble across all four datasets, achieving a pooled gain of $1.8$ points. We further evaluate five vision-language backbones across four datasets. Our method improves performance in $16$ of $20$ backbone--dataset combinations, with no significantly negative results. It also reduces pooled negative log-likelihood across all five backbones. Stronger text linking and transductive refinement provide no consistent improvements, suggesting that accurate visual class-name linking remains the main challenge. A second CLIP ViT-B/16 seed confirms the improvement on ImageNetV2, but not on ImageNet-A.

papers.title: Lightweight Spectral Subspace Filtering for Trojan-Resilient AI Inference Engines
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a significant security threat to deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on AI inference engines and hardware accelerators. By embedding hidden triggers during training, these attacks induce malicious behavior while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. Multi-trigger backdoor attacks are particularly challenging to detect and mitigate because of the distributed and stealthy nature of their effects. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a training-free Spectral Subspace Filtering framework that detects and suppresses backdoor-induced activations by analyzing latent feature representations. Exploiting the geometric separation between benign and malicious feature distributions, the framework employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify the dominant malicious subspace and performs inference-time spectral scrubbing through activation projection. This approach suppresses backdoor effects without model retraining, requiring only a small set of triggered samples collected offline. Experimental evaluation across CNN and transformer architectures, including AlexNet, ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNetV2, and Vision Transformer (ViT), demonstrates that the proposed method reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 94.2-99.8% to an average of 2.07%, while preserving clean accuracy of up to 98.54% with low inference overhead. The framework also demonstrates robustness across varying poisoning rates and multiple concurrent triggers, highlighting its potential as a lightweight runtime defense for enhancing the security and reliability of AI inference engines against backdoor attacks.

papers.title: Collision of a sphere and a prolate spheroid settling in a quiescent ambient
papers.abstract: The collision rate of a prolate spheroid and a sphere settling through a quiescent fluid at small Reynolds number is computed for randomly oriented spheroids and for spheroids turned broadside by weak fluid inertia. Without hydrodynamic interactions, the collision cross-section is the projection of the spheroid enlarged by the radius of the sphere. The ideal kernel then follows in closed form for aligned spheroids and from a one-dimensional quadrature for isotropic ones. Alignment raises the ideal kernel by at most a factor of 4/π, but extinguishes it on the extinction locus, where an isolated broadside spheroid settles as fast as the sphere. Hydrodynamic interactions are computed from pair trajectories in a first-reflection slender-body model, in which the interaction velocity is proportional to the difference of the buoyant weights and only the flow of the sphere rotates the spheroid. A strongly aligned spheroid weathervanes, whereas a freely rotating one feathers and glides. Weathervaning lowers the collision efficiency, as does feathering far from the extinction locus, but gliding raises it near the locus. There, the collision rate of spheroids aligned at a finite rate lies far above both the strong-alignment result and the ideal isotropic kernel. Just above the extinction locus, where strongly aligned spheroids are blocked, collisions persist at all the finite alignment rates computed. A boundary-element solution shows that the model overestimates the rate at which the gap closes near contact. A lubrication film largely corrects this and reduces the collision efficiencies from their interception values. Simple fits for the ideal kernels, the efficiencies and the near-contact correction are provided for use in collision models.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning from LLM-Generated (Suboptimal) Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved substantial progress across many domains, but training an agent \textit{tabula rasa} remains highly sample-inefficient. A common remedy is to initialize the agent using a neural network pretrained on demonstrations. However, collecting demonstrations is expensive, and the demonstrations themselves can be suboptimal. In this work, we use a large language model (LLM) to generate an advice policy that produces demonstration data with effectively no human cost. We use this data to warmstart a DQN agent, and use the advice policy itself to guide exploration during training. Because LLM-generated advice is often suboptimal, we further introduce a value warmstart method that initializes the agent to recognize promising states from the advice policy's behavior, without directly copying its actions. To characterize the robustness of this method, we systematically perturb individual sub-skills of an LLM-generated advice policy for a long-horizon, sparse-reward task. Degraded advice still meaningfully accelerates learning relative to unaided baselines. These results suggest that LLM-generated advice, though suboptimal, can be a cheap alternative to costly human demonstrations.

papers.title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
papers.abstract: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.

papers.title: What can a quantum network promise about the entangled pairs it delivers?
papers.abstract: Quantum networks will give users entangled pairs of qubits, the resource behind teleportation and quantum-secure keys. But a user cannot check a pair without destroying it, so networks promise the quality of each pair, its fidelity, from a physical model rather than from a measurement. If the model is too optimistic, the delivery rule alone may miss the error. We ask: what can a network actually guarantee? Our main result has two sides. By testing some pairs at random, in secret, users can put a lower bound on the average fidelity of the pairs they keep, without any model and at every moment. But when they test only a small fraction and keep most pairs, the tests cannot reliably show that every kept pair meets a fidelity threshold: a rare bad pair can still slip through. A promise about every single pair therefore rests on a model, and we give a rule that bounds each user's risk of ever receiving a bad pair under any data-driven routing, as long as the model is not optimistic or a large enough margin is declared in advance. Real data show calibration noise beyond chance, and in simulated networks a model error of the size seen in one experiment breaks the per-pair promise unless the margin was declared. On real data from trapped-ion and diamond links, the number of pairs decided how strong the certificate was: with about 3,000 pairs of a kilohertz link and 20% tested, the median certificate was 0.818, against the 0.817 we predicted in advance. We then ran the protocol ourselves on a 36-qubit trapped-ion processor in 50 pre-registered jobs. The certificate came within 0.003 of the measured fidelity, dropped by the predicted amount when we secretly damaged a third of the pairs, and, without changes, certified three- and four-qubit entangled states. The same tests also catch an optimistic model, but slowly. We pre-registered every confirmatory analysis and report the failures too.

papers.title: Rethinking Discovery Research with AI: The promise of transdisciplinarity and the danger of reductionism
papers.abstract: In theory, transdisciplinary research focuses on solving real-world problems without being constrained by disciplinary boundaries and methodologies. In practice, doing so is challenging, as recognized by the phrase "The world has problems; universities have departments." As a powerful integrative tool, AI may help overcome traditional reductionist approaches and enable genuine transdisciplinarity. In this essay, we discuss how this could happen and why, within the current system of incentives, it is not happening.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Imitation: Observation Conditioned Distillation for Video LLMs
papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

papers.title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline
papers.abstract: Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence. However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.

papers.title: Counting Eulerian Orientations in Regular Graphs
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a pseudograph, and let $\varepsilon(G)$ denote the number of Eulerian orientations of $G$. Lieb and Wu, and later Schrijver, showed that if $G$ has degree sequence $(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n)$, where each $d_i$ is a positive even integer, then \[ \varepsilon(G) \geq \prod_{i = 1}^n 2^{-d_i/2} \binom{d_i}{d_i/2}.\] Schrijver conjectured that for simple $d$-regular graphs, $\varepsilon(G)\leq\varepsilon(K_{d+1})^{n/(d+1)}$, with equality attained by disjoint unions of cliques of order $d+1$. In this paper, we prove a multigraph bound that implies the known case $d=4$, and we also improve Schrijver's lower bound for $d$-regular graphs, using an inductive relation between $\varepsilon(G)$ and the number $\ell_i(G)$ of cycles of each possible length $i \geq 1$ in $G$. We define \[ \ell(G) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \frac{\ell_i(G)}{(d - 1)^i}\] and we prove with $λ= (d - 1)\log(1 + 1/(d - 1))$ that for all $d \geq 2$, \[ \varepsilon(G) \geq \exp(λ\ell(G)) \cdot S_d(n),\] where $S_d(n)$ denotes $2^{-dn/2}\binom{d}{d/2}^n$. The bound sharply improves the lower bound of Lieb, Wu and Schrijver, and gives good estimates for $\varepsilon(G)$ for various graphs, such as integer lattices. The bound is almost tight for random regular graphs, and we conjecture for each even $d \geq 4$ that there exists a constant $c_d > 0$ such that $\varepsilon(G) \leq \exp(c_dλ\ell(G)) \cdot S_d(n)$ for every $n$-vertex $d$-regular pseudograph.

papers.title: Continuous-Time LQR from a Single Discrete-Time Off-Policy Batch
papers.abstract: We study discounted continuous-time linear--quadratic regulation (LQR) with unknown drift parameters and additive noise, using a single batch of discrete-time off-policy transitions. Discrete-time methods target a policy tied to the training interval, while shortening this interval can make learning from finite data more sensitive to noise. Learning an accurate continuous-time controller therefore requires balancing discretization and finite-sample errors while preserving stability throughout policy improvement. We develop a drift-only policy iteration algorithm, termed PhiBE-PI, using one quadratic state--action critic for policy evaluation and explicit greedy improvement. Reusing the batch makes later policies depend on the data. Exploiting the quadratic structure of LQR, we show that the data enter every policy evaluation only through one policy-independent empirical matrix, so a single high-probability bound controls all iterates. For sufficiently large discount~$β$, small observation intervals, and a sufficiently large batch, we prove that all iterates are stabilizing for the discounted problem and converge quadratically to a data-dependent fixed point. The gain bound separates iteration, finite-sample, and discretization errors. In this regime, the finite-sample and discretization terms scale as $1/(β\sqrt{nΔt})$ and $Δt/β$, respectively. The bounds thus reveal a tradeoff: at a fixed batch size, finer observations reduce discretization error but increase finite-sample error. Because PhiBE-PI approximates the continuous-time optimal gain rather than a discrete-time one, its policy can remain near-optimal when deployed at faster control rates. Experiments confirm this advantage over discrete-time Bellman-equation baselines when the observation interval is small relative to the system's time scale.

papers.title: Quantum-Annealing-Assisted Search-Space Reduction for Large-Scale Shortest-Path Computation
papers.abstract: Computing point-to-point shortest paths in large weighted graphs can require classical algorithms to explore a substantial portion of the graph. We ask whether quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) can reduce the work required to return a verified shortest path. For a known set of queries, we select paths that share arcs. For new queries, we select a corridor and test whether any path leaving it could improve the distance found by Dijkstra's algorithm. We also partition the graph into blocks and reuse local paths between their boundaries. We compare path encodings on identical inputs using simulated annealing on classical processors. The comparison of exact block overlays with direct Dijkstra search covered 45 synthetic graphs and the New York road network with 264,346 vertices. The overlay reduced the number of arc inspections in the final search in 97 of 200 graph and block-size combinations. Once endpoint attachment, assembly, and reconstruction were included, every combination took longer per query than direct Dijkstra search. On a separate set of 168 synthetic graphs, tightening the flow penalty increased the fraction of trials returning a verified local optimum within 20,ms from 35.8% to 84.1% under the same annealing schedule and update policy. A cost model for a prepared graph of 16,384 vertices predicts a 1.072x query speedup over a parallel classical overlay if five local problems can be solved accurately in one batch at the assumed service cost. The practical benefit of reduction thus depends on whether savings in the final search cover the cost of obtaining and verifying the local paths.

papers.title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification
papers.abstract: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.

papers.title: ReqSeek: Transformer-Based Automatic Requirements Identification for Building Large Requirements Datasets
papers.abstract: Large, diverse, and high-quality datasets are significant for advancing AI in requirements engineering, yet automated identification of requirements from Software Requirement Specifications (SRS) remains a challenge. Automatic Requirements Identification (ARI) methods demonstrate limited generalization to unseen documents across heterogeneous SRSs. This work presents ReqSeek, a transformer-based, domain-agnostic ARI model for recognizing ISO 29148-style requirements in SRS documents, supporting dataset construction. We curated the Automatic Requirements Identification Dataset (ARID), comprising 2,396 training instances from 23 heterogeneous SRSs, and fine-tuned four transformer architectures. RoBERTa was selected as the base model for ReqSeek and achieved 95% precision, recall, F1, and F0.89 on the held-out evaluation set. Exploratory human-model benchmarking showed performance comparable to humans while requiring substantially less prediction time than manual annotation. Post-hoc evaluation on out-of-domain (OoD) SRSs provided evidence of requirement identification beyond ARID. Robustness analysis demonstrated ReqSeek's insensitivity to minor linguistic variations while maintaining sensitivity to major ISO 29148-style violations. We applied ReqSeek to construct the Software Requirements Dataset (SwaRD), identifying 10,201 ISO 29148-style requirements from 231 industrial SRSs. SwaRD aligns with textual and semantic properties of human-curated datasets while exceeding them in scale and domain diversity. Our results suggest that transformer-based ARI can provide precise and generalizable requirements identification.

papers.title: LAF-ECG: Multi-Resolution Lead-Aware Fusion of Time-Series and Language Foundation Models for ECG Classification
papers.abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.

papers.title: Randomized Weighted Distance Nearest Neighbor Classification
papers.abstract: The nearest neighbor classifier is known to be memory-inefficient, and a popular solution is to compress its training data. Recently, a compression algorithm based on weighted distance nearest neighbor (WNN) was proposed, which has elegant theoretical properties and effective classification performance. However, its compression process is computationally expensive, for it performs a greedy search of the densest homogeneous balls in data space. In this paper, we propose a randomized variant RWNN. It simply randomizes the ball search process, and results in substantially reduced compression time (often 0.1%--1% of WNN's) and similar classification accuracy. RWNN also inherits several theoretical properties of WNN including consistency and a generalization bound. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate its efficacy.

papers.title: Interface currents of magnetized differential systems: quantization and bulk-interface correspondence
papers.abstract: This paper concerns transport along an interface between two insulators modeled by self-adjoint differential systems $H$ of arbitrary order, coupled to a magnetic field either by Peierls substitution or, for operators of the form $L^*L+W$, in the factor $L$. Each bulk carries a constant field, which may vanish. The principal symbol of $H$ is either elliptic or has a kernel of constant rank, in which case finitely many bands remain bounded at large momentum, as in rotating shallow water, cold plasmas, Maxwell's equations and pseudospin-one materials. Ellipticity is then replaced by a Douglis-Nirenberg structure and by a gap condition on an effective flat symbol. We show that, for every energy $α$ away from the flat-band set and in a spectral gap of both bulks, the interface current $σ_I=\mathrm{Tr}\,i[H,P]φ'(H)$ is well defined, with $2πσ_I$ a Fredholm index, and that it is given, for all walls in the elliptic case and under a freezing condition otherwise, by a bulk-interface correspondence of the form $2πσ_I=J(a_+,B_+;α)-J(a_-,B_-;α)+\mathsf{C}$. For a nonzero bulk field, $J=2πσ_H$ is the Kubo-Chern Hall conductivity, which we compute by an extension-corrected count of generalized Landau levels. For a vanishing field, $J$ is the Chern integral of the field-free symbol, which is also, under a weak-field condition, the weak-field limit of the Hall conductivity. The term $\mathsf{C}$ is a Chern integral of the occupied projector at infinite momentum across the wall. The current is stable under large perturbations, and boundaries of the applied field inside a homogeneous material carry quantized currents that change at field-induced transitions. Near flat-band energies, where generalized Landau levels may accumulate, the current may diverge.

papers.title: Unary maps are restrictions of linear maps and $k$-ary maps are restrictions of homogeneous maps
papers.abstract: We study maps on a finite set $S$ under renaming elements of $S$ and extending $S$. We show that every unary map is linear and every $k$-ary map is homogeneous with respect to such renamings and embeddings.

papers.title: Magic Production and the Fundamental Forces of Nature
papers.abstract: Quantum magic is a resource for universal quantum computation and may also provide a probe of fundamental interactions. We study its production in forward scattering of two distinct Standard Model fermions in the chirality basis. In the single-mediator-exchange approximation, magic production vanishes for gluon, photon, W-boson, Higgs-boson, and graviton exchange. For Z-boson exchange in purely leptonic scattering, it also vanishes at $\sin^2θ_W = 1/4$, close to the phenomenological value. By contrast, Z-boson exchange involving elementary quarks generally produces nonzero magic. These patterns raise the question of whether the construction of the fundamental forces encodes, at least in some channels, a tendency to suppress magic production.

papers.title: Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. It brings together tools for market analysis, forecasting, portfolio construction, and trading research through shared interfaces across models and agent frameworks. Agents can find suitable tools from natural-language requests, reuse tested implementations, and improve generated programs through checking and feedback. Developers can extend the library with new tools without rebuilding integrations for each model. Across 20 open-weight models on six trading-position tasks, tool discovery increased the proportion of episodes producing valid programs from 9.7% to 29.2%; for models with at least 14 billion parameters, it rose from 23.6% to 64.6%. We release the library and benchmark as a shared resource for the community and plan to expand its tools and task coverage as financial agents evolve.

papers.title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
papers.abstract: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.

papers.title: Occamy: A Semi-Oblivious Reconfigurable Datacenter Network
papers.abstract: Reconfigurable datacenter networks use fast circuit switches to provide high bandwidth at low cost, thereby emerging as a compelling alternative to packet switching. However, existing designs either react to fine-grained demand, requiring frequent optimization across the network, or remain completely demand-oblivious, requiring all-to-all connectivity that limits the cost benefits of circuit switching. We present Occamy, a semi-oblivious reconfigurable datacenter network that implements a tunable level of demand-fitting: it aggregates nodes into tunable-size clusters, and adapts a node-level circuit schedule to the coarse-grained demand between these clusters, thereby leveraging a demand-aware topology without frequent optimization overhead. Results on traditional cloud workloads and an AI training workload show that Occamy significantly improves the cost-performance tradeoff over state-of-the-art oblivious and demand-aware circuit-switched designs, while maintaining low overhead. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach using existing circuit-switched technology, implement an FPGA-based prototype, and evaluate failures.

papers.title: Lie Algebra Cohomology and Seiberg-Witten Theory
papers.abstract: We compute the algebra of perturbative holomorphic-topological local operators of pure $\mathcal N=2$ gauge theory with gauge group $SU(2)$, proving a conjecture of the author: it is the Poisson vertex algebra generated by a Virasoro element $X$ of central charge zero and an odd primary $Y$ of weight three, subject only to $X^2=0$. Equivalently, we compute the relative Lie algebra cohomology $H^*(\mathfrak{sl}_2[z,w]/(w^2),\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the self-Ext groups of the unit in the coherent Satake category for $SL_2$ and $PGL_2$. The proof uses factorization on configuration spaces of points on the affine line, a depth argument, and two deformations of the coefficient algebra $\mathbb C[z,w]/(w^2)$.

papers.title: UniDR: Learning To Generate Anatomical Deformations From Images via Unified Diffusion Modeling and Registration
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework, Unified Diffusion modeling and Registration (UniDR), which learns to generate arbitrary anatomical deformations from images with preserved topology. Existing approaches often model the generative process separately from registration-based deformation estimation; hence making them prone to propagated errors from the registration stage. To address this limitation, we propose a unified paradigm based on a conditional diffusion model over deformation fields that are jointly optimized from the registration process. A principled registration-guided score-matching objective function is then introduced to align the diffusion process with the deformation distribution induced by registration. As a result, our UniDR establishes an explicit connection between generation and registration: the diffusion model enables exploration of the space of plausible anatomical deformations, whereas registration provides structured supervision for learning transformations consistent with observed images. Once trained, UniDR is able to sample diverse, anatomically plausible transformations conditioned on any single input image. We evaluate UniDR across multiple real-world applications and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating high-fidelity image samples compared to the state-of-the-art. Additionally, we demonstrate that these generated samples improve performance in downstream medical image analysis and vision tasks.

papers.title: Learning-Augmented QUBO for Time-Expanded Multi-Commodity Flow
papers.abstract: We study energy-aware multi-commodity flow on time-expanded graphs, a problem that captures dynamic routing in layered networks and is NP-hard in general. We formulate the problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem, give an explicit penalty coefficient that provably guarantees feasibility, and show that it is smaller than the standard bound by a factor of roughly the number of active links. The layered structure of the time-expanded graph yields three structural results: a treewidth bound that gives a fixed-parameter tractable exact algorithm in the bag size, a matrix-product-operator representation of small bond dimension, and a proof that the annealing gap of the associated Ising Hamiltonian is strictly positive for every instance with a unique optimum, uniformly over bounded windows. For learning-augmented routing, we bound the Hamming distance between a predicted and an optimal flow by the flow error, and prove a consistency guarantee: a hybrid algorithm that keeps the better of the prediction and the solver output returns a flow whose cost exceeds the optimum by a factor that grows linearly with the prediction error. The results are exact statements about the QUBO and its associated Ising Hamiltonian, and they hold for any physical implementation.

papers.title: Accurate rank-controlled step-truncation methods for matrix differential equations
papers.abstract: A class of explicit time stepping schemes is introduced for the integration of matrix differential equations in low-rank format. These schemes combine explicit Runge-Kutta time stepping with rank-adaptive recompressions. For suitably chosen truncation thresholds, they converge at arbitrary order, while having close to optimal ranks, without any prior assumptions on the best approximation ranks. The ranks of the scheme also necessarily depend on the time step, as shown by counterexamples. A numerical experiment illustrates the advantages and performance of the proposed scheme.

papers.title: Cache the Knowledge, Not Just the Prompt: Dynamic Datalog as the Action Language for LLM Agents
authors: Bruno Rucy Carneiro Alves de Lima
papers.abstract: An LLM agent that answers questions about a knowledge graph writes a program per question, and its tools evaluate each from scratch. We give the agent a Datalog REPL, a session over a dynamic Datalog engine, in which rules are inserted and retracted like facts while derived facts stay current. Prompt caching reuses the model's processing of what a session shares, and the Datalog REPL reuses the evaluation of it. On chains of questions over three knowledge graphs, agents reuse a relation that the REPL keeps in 179 of 180 cases, with two models, and write fewer output tokens: SQL and Python agents write 23 to 82% more. With SQL tables or a Python namespace, Claude Haiku 5.5 stores almost nothing for later questions, and a chain of seven questions at 13 million facts takes it a median of 48 and 56 s, against 31 s with the REPL. Claude Opus 5.5 matches the REPL by storing tables in SQL, and when the data changes it stores views, which are evaluated again at every read. A relation that the REPL keeps is read like a table and stays current like a view. Datalog is a niche language beside SQL and Python, and with thinking enabled the models answer as accurately with it.

papers.title: Scheduling Algorithms for Millimeter-Wave Full-Duplex Integrated Access and Backhaul
papers.abstract: Integrated access and backhaul (IAB) is a cost-effective way to deploy millimeter-wave cellular networks, but under half-duplex (HD) operation, it exhibits poor latency and throughput scaling, as an IAB node's panels are typically scheduled to either all transmit or all receive in a given time slot to avoid self-interference. Upgrading IAB nodes with full-duplex capability (FD) allows their panels to be scheduled more flexibly, but doing so optimally across an entire network is challenging since self-interference couples link rates with scheduling decisions across nodes. In this work, we first develop a distributed dynamic programming algorithm that resolves this coupling by passing messages up and down the IAB tree, computing throughput-optimal back-pressure schedules in near-linear time. To reduce the control overhead associated with this approach, we also propose Floor-based Reduced-Overhead MaxWeight (FROM), which instead allows each node to schedule its panels independently of how its child nodes are scheduled. FROM accomplishes this by computing a floor on outgoing backhaul rates and scheduling each node using only local queue and channel states and its parent node's decision. We characterize the downlink stability region of this class of reduced-overhead policies and show that it spans at least half of the global stability region. We further prove that FROM stabilizes a guaranteed fraction of this region and identify conditions under which it achieves throughput optimality. Numerical results show that full-duplex IAB networks support higher traffic loads and lower delay than conventional half-duplex ones, and that FROM approaches the performance of global scheduling, even outperforming it when accounting for control overhead.

papers.title: Leray's Problem for the Stationary Navier-Stokes Equations with Low-Regularity Data in Planar and Three-Dimensional Axisymmetric Lipschitz Domains
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the steady Navier-Stokes Dirichlet problem in bounded planar and three-dimensional axisymmetric domains with finitely many disjoint Lipschitz boundary components. For prescribed velocities in $H^{1/2}(\partialΩ)$ and forces in the dual of the solenoidal energy space $V=H_0^1(\operatorname{div}0,Ω)$, we establish finite-energy solvability under the sole compatibility condition of zero total boundary flux. Individual component fluxes are subject to no smallness or sign restrictions. In three dimensions the domain and data are axisymmetric, and swirl is allowed. The result addresses the regularity of the domain and data within these two geometric classes. The proof combines Leray-Schauder continuation with pressure compactness on Lipschitz boundary collars and a total-head level-set argument. Continuation of the limiting Euler fields through complementary components supplies separating cycles, while viscous identities are evaluated inside the physical domain. A nonlinear correction of smooth force approximations controls the volume and surface errors in the passage to energy-dual data. An isometric extension from $V'$ to $H^{-1}$ preserves the prescribed symmetries and fixes the force representative used in the compactness argument. For each selected $H^{-1}$ representative, the resulting velocity admits an associated mean-zero $L^2$ pressure; the velocity equation depends only on the force class modulo gradients.

papers.title: Multiphase Gas in the Ram-Pressure-Stripped Elliptical Galaxy NGC 1404
papers.abstract: Galaxy groups and low-mass galaxy clusters are major sites of environment-driven galaxy evolution. NGC 1404 is an X-ray-bright early-type galaxy traveling through the intracluster medium of the nearby low-mass Fornax Cluster, and it hosts off-center warm ionized gas. With minimal ongoing stellar feedback and negligible active galactic nucleus feedback, NGC 1404 provides an ideal laboratory for constraining the impact of environmental processes on the thermodynamics of the interstellar medium. We analyzed VLT/MUSE, 506 ks Chandra ACIS, and 119 ks XMM-Newton RGS observations to quantify gas motions in both the hot and warm phases of NGC 1404. We probed the kinematics of the warm gas by deriving the velocity structure function (VSF) from MUSE H$α$ integral-field spectroscopy. To measure the kinematics of the hot gas, we derived the power spectrum of X-ray surface brightness fluctuations from the Chandra data, and independently constrained galaxy-scale hot gas motions by measuring Fe XVII resonant scattering and turbulent line broadening with RGS. Our RGS spectral analysis gives a three-dimensional Mach number of $0.48^{+0.22}_{-0.14}$, consistent with the power-spectrum results from Chandra for the same extraction region, and corresponding to a turbulent-to-thermal energy density ratio of $\sim0.13$. The warm-gas VSF follows the expectation for Kolmogorov turbulence and is broadly consistent with the hot-gas kinematics. The off-center warm gas in NGC 1404 may have formed through radiative cooling of the hot interstellar medium, triggered by the uplift of low-entropy hot gas during ram pressure stripping. Our study suggests that ram pressure stripping can drive substantial gas motions and reshape the thermodynamic state of the interstellar medium of cluster member galaxies.

papers.title: Around the base ideal and the base locus of a Keller map
papers.abstract: Let $φ_F:\Bbbk^n\to\Bbbk^n$ be a Keller map defined by $n$ polynomials $F_1,\ldots,F_n$ in $n$ indeterminates $X=X_1,\ldots,X_n$ over a field $\Bbbk$ of characteristic zero. Miranda-Neto defined the base ideal of $φ_F$ as the ideal $I_F$ generated by $F_1,\ldots,F_n$ and the base locus of $φ_F$ as the affine algebraic set $V_F=V(I_F)$ determined by the ideal $I_F$. He proved that $I_F$ is a radical ideal, which is a finite intersection of $v_F$ maximal ideals, where ${\rm card}(V_F)\leq v_F$, understanding that $v_F=0$, when $I_F$ is improper. In this paper, we first prove that $v_F\leq \dim_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk[X]/I_F)\leq [\Bbbk(X):\Bbbk(F)]$. Using invertible affine transformations on the recent counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture announced by Alpöge, we show that $I_F$ might indeed be improper and that the following cases, $0<{\rm card}(V_F)=v_F<[\Bbbk(X):\Bbbk(F)]$, $0<{\rm card}(V_F)=v_F=[\Bbbk(X):\Bbbk(F)]$, $0<{\rm card}(V_F)<v_F<[\Bbbk(X):\Bbbk(F)]$ and $0={\rm card}(V_F)<v_F<[\Bbbk(X):\Bbbk(F)]$ might occur. We finish by giving a purely topological equivalent reformulation of the Jacobian Conjecture in terms of the irreducibility of $V_F$.

papers.title: Loop-Count Schedules in Looped Transformers: An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Looped transformers apply one block of layers several times with shared weights, trading parameters for repeated computation. We study how the schedule of the loop iteration count R during training determines whether each extra pass acts as a full layer or as a small correction, using a controlled ladder of 46M-110M-parameter models trained on 2B tokens with learned residual gates on every loop pass and three schedules: R fixed to 2, R sampled uniformly from {1,...,6}, and R sampled from {2,3,4}. We find that the lower bound of the sampling range is the decisive choice. If the sampled range includes R=1, so that some training steps run the block only once and compute the loss on that single pass, the gates collapse to 0.1-0.5 and each additional pass becomes a small correction to the first; if the range starts at R=2, so that every training step runs the block at least twice, the gates stay at 0.6-0.9 and each pass keeps the strength of a full layer, while the model can still be run at any R from 2 up to twice the largest trained value with validation loss within a few hundredths of a nat of its best. The {2, 3, 4} schedule gives the best looped model, 2.909 nats against 2.951 for the parameter-matched plain model, and degrades by only 0.038 nats when run at twice its trained depth. We further show that under a fixed R the direction of the residual stream converges geometrically beyond the trained depth while the loss diverges, which refines a recent finding that static-depth training does not converge, and that reusing the first pass's keys and values on later passes costs 0.01-0.03 nats in every regime while making the per-token iteration uniformly contractive and halving the inference cache. The loop recovers about a third of what real depth provides at equal parameters. The code, trained weights, and per-token traces are released.

papers.title: A high-dimensional perspective of assortative mating: definition, dynamics, and limiting results
papers.abstract: Assortative mating, or the systematic (dis)similarity of traits between mate pairs, has wide-ranging consequences. Chiefly, it modulates genetic variance in offspring due to the coupling of inherited trait-associated loci in parents. Over many generations, this buildup becomes appreciable at the trait level and may confound statistical genetics techniques, such as association analyses and heritability estimation. Theoretical characterisations of this effect are well-developed in the univariate case, where mates assort on a single trait pair. However, empirical studies increasingly show that assortment is not only multivariate, but high-dimensional, in that the correlation structure exhibited between mates cannot be represented by a single or few linear combinations of the constituent traits. In spite of this, the mathematical theory of assortment has not scaled with awareness of this fact. In this paper such a generalisation is developed. We begin by deriving sufficient conditions under which an estimator is invariant to assortment, followed by studying existence conditions and limiting behaviour of equilibria under assortment. Finally, univariate results involving trait heritability and consanguineal genetic correlation are generalised to the multivariate regime.

papers.title: Unresolved binaries from Gaia XP to SPHEREx
papers.abstract: Unresolved companions alter the luminosity and spectra of a star, but a colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) reveals them only when the system is over-luminous, and a Gaia photocentre orbit constrains only a combination of the mass and flux ratios. We fit the absolute Gaia BP/RP (XP) and SPHEREx spectra (XPS) of about 71,000 low-mass stars in the Gaia Catalogue of Nearby Stars with the J-CaPS XPS emulator, which predicts single-star and coeval-binary spectra on an absolute flux scale. First, more than half of known binaries lie within the main-sequence (MS) band of the CMD, because the companion is faint or lifts a metal-poor primary onto the single-star ridge. XPS recovers 86 per cent of the binaries that a CMD cut finds and 44 per cent of those it misses. Second, a small photocentre motion can come from a faint companion or a luminous one of nearly equal mass. XPS distinguishes them and recovers the mass ratios of double-lined binaries. Among substellar candidates with radial-velocity follow-up, it ranks all 11 binaries above all 16 confirmed brown-dwarf or planet hosts. The public package spbin provides this check before follow-up. Third, where XPS detects no companion light, we place an upper limit on the light of an MS companion. Among Gaia DR3 astrometric orbits with clean spectral fits, 2841 require more companion mass than XPS allows for a single MS star. Within 200 pc, their companion masses cluster at those of typical white dwarfs, and nearly circular orbits support this interpretation. Of 24 companions that joint radial-velocity and astrometric orbits show to be faint, XPS recovers 22, compared with 14 selected by the absence of a colour excess. Applied to forthcoming Gaia DR4 orbital solutions, XPS can help distinguish luminous binaries from substellar companions and identify candidate compact companions whose dynamical masses exceed the limits allowed by their light.

papers.title: Two-loop correction to the complex-bion amplitude in a quasi-exactly solvable sextic oscillator
papers.abstract: In this study, a quasi-exactly solvable sextic potential is analyzed by two diagrammatic calculations.
