papers.abstract: Platform studies show that generative AI has reduced demand for freelance writing and image work, and experiments show that it makes individual workers faster. This letter asks how these two findings look to workers who are both users of the technology and exposed to it. I analyze 30 interviews with Bangladeshi online freelancers, conducted in Bangla between May and August 2025. Twenty-one participants used generative AI in their own work, sixteen said that it was replacing freelance work, and thirteen said both. Eleven of the sixteen placed replacement on others: on beginners and workers who do not update their skills, on "basic" tasks, or on other sectors. Participants also described how prices fell as tasks became faster, and how clients cited AI to offer less. I propose the term adoption bind for this pattern: each worker adopts generative AI to stay on the safe side of the line, while the same tools, in the hands of competitors and clients, lower what the market pays for the work. The bind suggests that productivity gains measured for individuals can become price losses for workers as a group, and that these losses fall first on entry-level work.

papers.title: Modeling extraordinary relativistic jets on the scale of the cosmic web
papers.abstract: Recent observations of supermassive black hole jets extending up to the typical sizes of cosmic web filaments challenge our current understanding. In particular, the overall jet size of J152932.16+601534.4 ("Porphyrion") reaches $\sim 7$ Mpc at redshift 0.896. Magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) models of relativistic jets have never been successfully applied to such extraordinary distances, requiring demanding jet-environment and flow stability conditions. By using state-of-the-art numerical simulations of 3D relativistic-MHD jets, we show that Porphyrion's observational properties can be successfully modelled in a realistic scenario, involving a jet kinetic power of $3.5 \times 10^{46}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and an external medium of a low-density galaxy group. We find that the pair of jets expands to $\sim 9$ Mpc in about $20$ Myr, implying that the jet grows with relativistic speeds for most of its evolution. Comparing this case with other jets of similar power propagating in substantially denser cosmic structures, we find much slower outflows that can only reach a few Mpc, consistent with the bulk of the observed population of giant radio galaxies. Our results make a testable prediction, i.e. future detections of even larger-scale jets in upcoming surveys and database searches will be invaluable in studying the demographics and feedback of the poorly known population of powerful jets, particularly in under-dense regions of the cosmic web.

papers.title: Loadability Assessment for Large-Load Integration: From Repeated Power Flow Tracing to Historical Trajectory Transfer
papers.abstract: Integrating large data-center loads requires utilities to evaluate voltage-stability loading margins under different generation and demand conditions. Continuation power flow (CPF) traces P--V curves through successive prediction and correction steps, but related assessments can repeatedly reconstruct similar nonlinear behavior. Reusing an operating point as an initial guess does not capture the subsequent voltage response. This paper proposes a continuation method that transfers finite segments of historical power flow (PF) trajectories. Each segment is aligned with the present state and continuation direction, supplementing the CPF tangent predictor with previously computed nonlinear curve shape. Short Newton tests evaluate compatibility with the present PF equations, and an attention-based selector combines their results with network conditions, loading patterns, and recent continuation states. Numerical correction and fold refinement determine accepted solutions and the loading limit. The analysis bounds prediction error through differences in trajectory curvature and establishes sufficient conditions for local correction and branch preservation. Studies on modified IEEE 14- and 118-bus systems under renewable-generation and data-center load variations demonstrate reduced online computation and higher observed recovery of specified continuation solutions than Adaptive CPF. For loading-limit assessment, paired online speedups are 4.88--21.62$\times$ over Adaptive CPF and 1.53--4.77$\times$ over holomorphic embedding with arc-length parametrization (HEAP) across the tested scenarios.

papers.title: Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories. PULSE constructs deterministic, time-indexed project state and documented collaborator views from source-linked records, and evaluates three families of questions: open loops, project evolution, and view gaps. Across retrieval agents, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle conditions, we find substantial headroom for current systems. Retrieval and extraction account for the largest share of the gap, but providing explicit project state on top of gold evidence yields further substantial gains, showing that PPSU cannot be reduced to retrieval alone. Further analysis shows that questions requiring information to be reconciled across multiple parts of the project history remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided, while project-state synthesis and perspective conditioning remain persistent challenges. These results motivate enterprise agents that explicitly maintain and reconcile temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.

papers.title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
papers.abstract: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

papers.title: Treatment Policy Design in the Presence of Measurement Error
papers.abstract: In many applications, treatments are assigned based on unit features, leading to personalized treatment policies. This often involves optimizing objective functions with counterfactual quantities such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). In practice, some key features may be measured with error and ignoring such errors can introduce systematic bias. We study how to design personalized treatment policies when some features are latent and only noisy measurements are available. We ask how policies can be constructed when the CATE is not identifiable, and how uncertainty from measurement error can be incorporated into policy design. We propose two frameworks for treatment policy design based on partial identification, focusing on the measurement mechanism-the conditional distribution of observed measurements given unobserved features. The first framework builds on ideas from proximal causal inference. The second adopts a modular Bayesian approach based on a reparameterized likelihood, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Bayesian regression models to separately perform posterior inference on the measurement mechanism and nuisance functions. Posterior quantiles are then used to construct credible intervals for the CATE that account for uncertainty in both components. Treatment policies are then derived by comparing the null value of the CATE to these bounds. The proposed methods provide a coherent way to account for measurement error and model uncertainty in personalized treatment policy design.

papers.title: How a Prediction Dies: A Challenge-Driven, Rule-Bound Self-Refutation in an LLM Agent Society
papers.abstract: Persistent societies of large language model agents now make empirical claims about their own collective behaviour, yet the fate of such claims is rarely observable. We document one claim, from registration to death, on AITRAP, a multi-agent platform whose public, append-only ledger records every action. The claim (0495d171, registered 19 October 2026) asserted that a majority of bridges between problem domains would remain attached to a single exploration lineage. Three community challenges forced its judgment criterion through four versions, from an ambiguous statement to an executable protocol with a fixed threshold, a minimum-frame-size gate, and a baseline calibration gate. When the first frame with at least 20 bridges arrived, support stood at 9 of 79 (11.4%; Wilson 95% CI [6.1%, 20.3%]); the author, bound by the registered clause, refuted the claim and relinquished the associated stake. Three findings emerge. The criterion became executable only under community pressure, which we document version by version. The calibration gate caught a fault in the author's own recalculation that would otherwise have published a spuriously perfect 0/79 result. The failure itself traces to a denominator that grew 8.8-fold in five days while the numerator grew 1.8-fold, coinciding with a change in platform incentives; we report this mechanism as a hypothesis, not a rescuing condition. A claim whose termination is carried out exactly as written carries more evidential weight than one that survives, and this case provides initial empirical grounds for treating voluntary self-refutation as a candidate indicator of epistemic accountability in incentive-coupled agent societies.

papers.title: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD
papers.abstract: Decentralized SGD minimizes a common objective by local gradient steps and neighbor averaging. Its statistical theory mostly concerns network averages, yet clients act on their own iterates, and one-sided decisions such as alarms use one tail of the local error. We show that a client's constant-step endpoint can have nearly nominal Gaussian coverage while both tails are badly miscalibrated. An exact noise-filter representation explains why: a quantity computable from the graph and stepsize decides whether the endpoint is asymptotically Gaussian, and when the number of clients outgrows the inverse stepsize on networks with summable return probabilities, such as lazy tori of dimension at least three and expanders, a few recent noise terms at nearby clients keep a fixed share of local variance. On these tori the limit is a non-Gaussian local field plus an independent Gaussian consensus term, and no reference distribution built from finitely many noise moments, including Edgeworth and Cornish--Fisher corrections, is calibrated at all levels uniformly over noise laws. We propose a hybrid reference that resamples the influential noise terms from their empirical law and replaces the rest by a Gaussian; its non-asymptotic coverage bound allows noise laws and curvature estimated from fresh gradients or the client's trajectory, and extends to nonlinear vector objectives. In full-network simulations it restores tail balance at essentially unchanged interval length, also under rare large shocks that break Cornish--Fisher intervals; gains vanish, as predicted, when consensus dominates.

papers.title: CausalNTP: A World-Model Recipe for Causal Next-Token Prediction under Noisy Training-data
papers.abstract: This paper shows that transformer networks trained with next-token prediction (NTP) and gradient descent do not learn to make predictions using only causally-relevant tokens in the left context, irrespective of the causal ordering of tokens during training, and identifies the learning deficiencies responsible. We introduce a causal world-model setup, for which, we characterize the Bayes-optimal predictor under the causal view of the data. We then prove that, a function that distills its predictions to non-causal views of data, when realized under Occam's Razor, recovers the true causal predictor. Based on this analysis we propose CausalNTP, a practical training algorithm that approximates this theoretical recipe and trains transformers to depend only the causally relevant tokens in left-context. Empirically in the world-model setup, CausalNTP achieves out-of-distribution generalization that vanilla NTP cannot due to its theoretical limits, regardless of data and model scale. We show similar gains and behavior in the natural language question-answering setting as a proof-of-concept.

papers.title: Schedule, Rank, Profile: Continuous Evaluation of LLM Agents in Games
papers.abstract: Games are a robust test for large language model agents: they require sequential decisions, adversarial or cooperative interaction, state tracking, reasoning under uncertainty, and long-horizon planning. However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

papers.title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence
papers.abstract: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. Their inputs are serially dependent, yet existing guarantees largely assume independence. We show that dependence creates a directional bias that score autocovariances cannot detect: reversing a stationary stream leaves every score autocovariance unchanged but can change the leading bias threefold. For finite memory and decreasing stepsizes, the bias splits into lag-specific interactions between the threshold and the current observation and a curvature term; delaying the threshold removes the interactions one lag at a time while keeping every observation and the leading variance. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. Testing fixed candidates instead keeps the score centered, so calibration depends only on score autocovariances. Extending local-dependence self-normalized approximations to the implemented acceptance hull, we show that inverting these tests gives a density-free, moment-free interval for the population quantile with $O(n^{-1/2})$ coverage error for a fixed sufficient lag window, a rate that is sharp for this interval, and a guarantee for data-selected windows; an exact scan takes $O(n\log n)$ time. Experiments confirm the lag-by-lag predictions and show calibration competitive with block bootstrap at lower cost.

papers.title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
papers.abstract: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

papers.title: Who Gets Blamed for the Blackout? A Critical Incident Analysis of Clients, Reputation Systems, and Online Freelancers
papers.abstract: Online labor platforms such as Fiverr and Upwork judge freelancers by how fast they reply, whether they deliver on time, and what clients say about them. In the Global South, these signals depend on electricity and internet connections that workers do not control. This paper asks how infrastructure failures, such as power outages, internet failures, and government internet shutdowns, become lasting reputational penalties in the gig economy, and how freelancers prevent or repair them. We use the critical incident technique to analyze 149 incidents from 30 interviews with online freelancers in Bangladesh, including accounts of the July 2024 nationwide internet shutdown. Most breakdowns were absorbed without lasting harm. Of the 21 that became lasting penalties, 17 passed through clients. A client who could not see the power cut or the shutdown read the worker's silence as unreliability and left, canceled, or gave a bad rating. Platform reputation systems then stored that judgment without its context. We call this two-stage process client-mediated misattribution. Freelancers responded with four repair strategies: making the context visible, making the breakdown invisible, staying visible to the platform, and reducing dependence on any single platform or client. Exposure and the capacity to repair were unequal, and urban participants were the most exposed. The study extends research on algorithmic management, attribution in distributed work, and information and communication technologies for development (ICT4D), and it proposes outage-aware design for platform rating and reputation systems.

papers.title: Inverse design of polarization-analyzing gratings
papers.abstract: Metasurface polarization analyzing gratings have attracted increasing interest for polarization management and sensing in optical systems. Traditional strategies for the design of these gratings are based on a formalism combining the Jones calculus with Fourier optics. While this approach has achieved notable success in numerous applications, its validity is restricted to the paraxial regime. Here we introduce a differentiable topology optimization framework for these gratings which is free of this constraint. We show that this framework can yield designs which outperform the traditional approach, especially at high angles. Additionally, we provide preliminary experimental validation to corroborate these results.

papers.title: Topology-Preserving Hodge--Laplacian Diffusion on Manifolds with Boundary
papers.abstract: Overview: We study deterministic and stochastic Hodge--Laplacian diffusion of differential forms on a fixed smooth compact Riemannian manifold with boundary. Absolute and relative boundary conditions select harmonic spaces representing ordinary and relative cohomology. We investigate the preservation properties of these diffusion processes, their compatible cellular discretizations, and their implications for reverse diffusion models. Numerical experiments on an annulus and a solid torus illustrate the theoretical results. Mathematical Significance: Using the de Rham complex and its constant-sheaf interpretation, we distinguish preservation of harmonic coordinates from preservation of a cohomology class. We establish that deterministic heat flow preserves the harmonic projection and exponentially damps its orthogonal complement. For additive stochastic forcing, we prove that pathwise harmonic preservation is equivalent to the absence of harmonic noise. Exact forcing preserves closedness and the initial cohomology class for closed initial data, whereas harmonic-projected forcing need not preserve closedness. We further show that compatible cellular discretizations retain these properties, with an algebraic extension to fixed weighted cellular sheaves. Separating invariant preservation from time-step stability and covariance accuracy, we derive bounds on leakage arising from approximate harmonic projectors. AI Relevance: We develop a finite-dimensional conditional score formulation that confines reverse diffusion to a prescribed harmonic component or, for closed data, a fixed cohomology class. This provides a mathematically grounded framework for incorporating topological constraints into diffusion-based generative AI models on manifolds.

papers.title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Designing mechanical metamaterials for nonlinear behavior such as energy absorption is limited by high-dimensional parametrizations and by expensive simulations. Here we show that design knowledge from a cheap linear property can be transferred to nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable, targets through a learned, reusable search space. TRAMA (TRAnsferable representation learning for Metamaterial Architectures) reparametrizes architected materials using a variational autoencoder with a pre-trained vision transformer and physics-informed augmentations. For energy-absorption efficiency, TRAMA reaches every efficiency level with 95 to 98% reduction in the evaluations needed by state-of-the-art gradient-free optimization and 3 to 5 fewer than gradient-based optimization. Its best design is comparable to the best found by any baseline with at least 67% fewer evaluations, which translate into approximately 100 hours saved per campaign with finite-element simulations. Fabricated designs match simulated stress-strain curves within 5.3%. A post hoc analysis shows where the representation transfers to new properties and where it does not.

papers.title: Incompressible quantum information
papers.abstract: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.

papers.title: Triangle decompositions of two-dimensional simplicial complexes
papers.abstract: We study fractional triangle decompositions of two-dimensional simplicial complexes, unifying the settings of Nash-Williams' conjecture on triangle decompositions and the high-dimensional Dirac problem for Steiner triple systems. We prove that every sufficiently large two-dimensional simplicial complex with minimum degree at least $(1-d_1)n$ and maximum missing codegree at most $d_2n$ admits a fractional triangle decomposition, provided $d_1/0.21+d_2/0.27\leq 1$. As an immediate consequence, we prove the asymptotic form of Lee's high-dimensional Dirac conjecture: every sufficiently large admissible $3$-uniform hypergraph with minimum codegree at least $(3/4+\varepsilon)n$ contains a Steiner triple system. We also provide constructions establishing lower bounds on this fractional decomposition threshold problem.

papers.title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation via Dual-Branch Supervision
papers.abstract: For on-policy distillation (OPD), more capable models are a natural choice as teachers. However, higher task performance does not necessarily imply greater teachability. A controlled token intervention study suggests that even a model weaker than the student can serve as an informative contrastive reference. Building on this observation, we propose Contrastive On-Policy Distillation (cOPD), which provides dual branch supervision by contrasting strong teacher, weak teacher, and student predictions at student generated prefixes. Our analysis explains how this three way comparison helps select token candidates associated with better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model. We evaluate cOPD across diverse teacher student configurations spanning different training stages, parameter scales, and model families, on tasks including mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and question answering with abstention. cOPD achieves the best or top-tier performance among the evaluated baselines across all three tasks, improving overall Pass@16 on mathematical reasoning by up to 7.51\% over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and suggest that it facilitates exploration.

papers.title: Exploring new speciation patterns: architecture of genetic similarity networks
papers.abstract: We use an individual based model to identify signatures of speciation modes in genetic similarity networks. These networks group individuals based on their genetic similarity, defined through Hamming distances between binary strings representing their genomes. The results of our extensive simulations demonstrate that sympatric and parapatric speciation modes are clearly distinguishable and measurable through specific network metrics. In particular, structural properties -- including clustering coefficient, mean degree, geodesic distance, and assortativity -- show significant differences in both stationary values and transient phases, giving rise to a novel framework for distinguishing between speciation modes.

papers.title: Competing climates of the present-day Earth: from Snowball to Hothouse
papers.abstract: Earth today has one climate, but it could have others. With the same continents, the same solar constant and the same pre-industrial CO2, our planet could settle into strikingly different ones. We explore this possibility with BIG-MITgcm, a model which couples atmosphere and ocean circulation with ice sheets and vegetation, and which can be integrated over many millennia. We find five different climates and describe them here. At one extreme is a Snowball, with ice from pole to pole. A Waterbelt also exists, in which sea ice reaches the tropics and only a thin equatorial ribbon of open ocean survives. There is a Cold world much like the Last Glacial Maximum, a Warm climate in which we live in today, and a Hot world in which the Atlantic overturning circulation has collapsed. Each state is held in place by its own balance of competing feedbacks. Ocean heat transport anchors each climate, holding the ice edge where that transport is weak. The familiar climate of the past 10 thousand years is perhaps just one of several possibilities. This has implications for glacial-interglacial transitions and the risk of crossing global tipping points in the future.

papers.title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

papers.title: Real-time event-level zero-shot learning at 150 ns: towards a foundation model for particle physics experiment triggering
papers.abstract: The hardware-based Level-1 triggers of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments select collisions with algorithms designed for one signature each, acting on a coarse, low-latency view of every event. We present a learned event embedding for several trigger tasks and evaluate its transfer to processes absent from training. Using paired offline and Level-1 views of the same simulated collisions, we train an offline transformer with a supervised metric loss and distil it, event by event, into a quantised Level-1 transformer whose bit widths are learned under a fixed resource budget. Trained on 25 Standard Model processes, the embedding places 28 held-out processes next to their physical relatives. A nearest-neighbour selection against background collisions, which never enter encoder training, rejects 99% of them. It retains a median of 90% of seen and 96% of unseen Standard Model events and 88% of a set of 52 beyond-the-Standard-Model benchmark samples, the best-performing score across the three groups among the baselines evaluated on the same events. A second gate against the seen processes isolates high-mass dilepton signals into label-free clusters, and long-lived signals too when displaced-track information is available. With 7512 parameters and an FPGA latency of 147 ns, the encoder uses one event representation, learned once, to derive several selections, opening the door to a foundation model for the LHC's hardware-based triggers.

papers.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.

papers.title: Tailored Magic States for Algorithmic Primitives
papers.abstract: Algorithmic primitives such as adders, multipliers, and Boolean logic typically contain clusters of multi-qubit non-Clifford gates, whose decomposition into $T$ and $CCZ$ gates adds scheduling and spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Synthillation addresses this difficulty for diagonal circuits at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy by jointly synthesizing and distilling their non-Clifford content. In this work, we develop a complementary, code-theoretic approach to synthillation. We introduce CSS-T-Product (CSS-TP) codes, whose transversal single-qubit phase gates implement multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and give analytical rules that predict these logical gates from tensor-network operations. Using quantum LEGO, we generate code families with logical actions at the third and fourth levels of the Clifford hierarchy. We classify the resulting resource states as canonical (such as $T$ or $CCZ$), tensor products of canonical states, or irreducible, i.e., not reducible to a product of non-Clifford gates via Clifford operations and logical basis changes. Conversion into Encode-$T$-Decode factories built from these codes recover known synthillation resources and prepare magic states at higher levels of the Clifford hierarchy; we analyze them with a surface-code-based model for several algorithmic primitives. We demonstrate that tailored magic factories give significant latency improvements at similar or smaller occupied spacetime volume: at code distance $21$ with one factory per resource family, they reduce the latency of a $GF(2^{8})$ multiplier and a shared-addend carry-lookahead adder by up to $48\%$ and $38\%$, respectively, and the smallest tailored factory also lowers the occupied spacetime volume. CSS-TP codes thus connect code construction to resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives.

papers.title: Norm-attaining operators on renormings of $c_0$
papers.abstract: We study norm-attaining operators on three renormings of $c_0$: Read's space $\Read$, its smooth renorming $\sRead$, and Martín's space $\X$. We prove that, for every Banach space $F$ and every $Z\in\{\Read,\sRead\}$, norm-attaining finite-rank operators are dense in $\K(Z,F)$. Consequently, $\NA(Z,F)$ is dense in $\Lin(Z,F)$ whenever $F$ is reflexive. More generally, we establish that the compact Hilbertian smoothing construction of Debs, Godefroy and Saint-Raymond \cite{DGS} preserves the density of norm-attaining operators for all finite-dimensional ranges. We also extend a second-order criterion of Kadets, López-Pérez, Martín and Werner \cite{KLMWfr} from rank two to arbitrary ranks $k\geq 2$ for operators into $\ell_2^k$, and prove that the same smoothing preserves the existence and non-existence of such operators. We further investigate the possibilities and limitations of renorming techniques for excluding rank-two norm-attaining operators through analytical and geometrical approaches, including constructions that preserve the set of norm-attaining functionals. For Martín's space $\X$, we prove that, for every Banach space $F$ and every integer $1\leq k\leq\dim F$, there exists a rank $k$ norm-attaining operator from $\X$ into $F$, answering a question of Martín \cite{Mar}. We also show that, for every nonzero Banach space $F$, $\K(\X,F)$ contains a norm-dense linear subspace whose nonzero elements fail to attain their norms.

papers.title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
papers.abstract: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

papers.title: Two Actions from One State: Fork Futures Teach JEPA World Models to Compare
papers.abstract: JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. The logged behavior data show one action per state, and under a local linear approximation we prove the action response is unidentified along any direction the policy never varies within a state. We therefore supplement behavior data with measured outcomes of alternative actions from the same state. Our fork futures execute two actions from one restored state, and their outcome difference cancels the state term, identifying the action response on the sampled span. The resulting model, Fork-JEPA, matches predicted to measured differences, anchors the logged successor with behavior prediction, and adds a lookback head that keeps the predecessor recoverable, all at training time, leaving planning unchanged. On three visual control tasks, behavior-only training leaves the predicted action effect no better than a constant guess. Fork-JEPA makes it readable and raises planning success by up to 14\% over LeWM, its base model. Where the action response changes across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success, and 1,024 fork pairs beat 1.2M extra behavior steps. Our project is available at https://fork-jepa.github.io/.

papers.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
papers.abstract: Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.

papers.title: SMAD: A Semantics-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. A semantics-aware ensemble integrates validated candidates and attributes each alert to contributing detectors and supporting evidence. On univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, SMAD improves detection performance over the strongest baseline by 11.5% and 9.6%, respectively, while outperforming general-purpose coding agents at 2-5x lower language-model token cost.

papers.title: Wireless readout and control of cavity magnon-polaritons via photonic modes delocalised across a gap
papers.abstract: In cavity magnonics, photon-magnon hybridisation is typically detected by measuring the cavity response (i.e. measuring cavity resonance shifts through its reflection or transmission spectra). While a large body of work in the field has focused on three-dimensional cavities, a variety of two-dimensional resonators have also been explored as hosts for photonic modes due to their compatibility with on-chip integration. Nevertheless, the readout approach remains largely unchanged. Here, we demonstrate remote excitation and readout of cavity magnon-polaritons using two spatially separated, wirelessly coupled ring resonators. Through inductive coupling, energy is transferred between the resonators, enabling the magnonic system to be excited by one resonator while its hybrid-mode spectrum is detected through measurements of the other. We demonstrate wireless readout of cavity magnon-polaritons at separations ranging from millimetres to centimetres, identifying their characteristic response in the remotely measured spectrum. This establishes wireless resonator coupling as a route to remote interrogation of hybrid photon-magnon systems.

papers.title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

papers.title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
papers.abstract: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

papers.title: Enabling Verifiable Output Lineage for Virtualized ML Workload Execution
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) property attestation lets a model provider demonstrate properties of their models and datasets to verifiers, and trusted execution environments (TEEs) have emerged as its most practical mechanism. However, existing TEE-based systems attest only a static snapshot of the TEE's initial configuration, leaving run-time behavior unauditable. Proof of execution (PoX) architectures close this gap by requiring the prover's root of trust to also demonstrate that (1) the attested operation actually executed and (2) the claimed outputs were affected only by that operation. Existing PoX designs, though, target microcontrollers and rely on hardware features unavailable in server-grade TEEs, so they cannot be applied directly to ML workloads. We present EVOLVE, a software-based PoX framework for server-grade TEEs. EVOLVE mediates an operation's writes and control flow to track whether a requested ML operation executes without violation. It binds the execution status to measurements of the operation's inputs and outputs, enabling verifiers to assess run-time behavior through ML property attestation. We implement EVOLVE on Intel TDX as a Rust module within its virtual firmware, with policy checks built on primitives formally verified in F*. Our evaluation shows that EVOLVE is versatile across diverse ML applications on unmodified hardware, provides formal guarantees for its policy checks. EVOLVE incurs per-request run-time overhead on average ranging from 1.07$\times$ (for decision trees) to 2.13$\times$ (for multi-layer perceptrons).

papers.title: Multiplicity of Normal A-Type Field Stars of Low Projected Rotational Velocity
papers.abstract: While nearly all rapidly rotating (vsini > 120 km/s) A stars are observed to have normal spectra, a significant fraction (~43%) of slow rotators have peculiar spectra although many do not. For over 30 years, we conducted a radial velocity survey of 119 non-peculiar, slowly rotating dwarf or subgiant A stars. We determined orbital elements and related parameters for 43 systems and along with known visual binaries, common proper motion companions and stars with proper motion anomalies, find a multiplicity fraction of 0.64. We compared our results to recent findings concerning similar stars. We also examined whether the slow rotation of our sample of could have been caused by tidal interactions in short-period binaries. Of the 80 stars that we determined to be at least binary in nature or to show other evidence of having companions, only 6 have periods < 10 days. Thus, a large majority have periods that are much too long for tidal forces to have reduced their rotation rates while they are on the main-sequence. We also observed a small sample of rapid rotators (vsini = 125-230 km/s) over a shorter time interval to judge the accuracy of our measuring techniques on A stars with very broad lines. Orbital elements for 5 non-survey A-type stars, also with low vsini, are listed with our results, but are not included in the statistical discussion.

papers.title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
papers.abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

papers.title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

papers.title: Enumerative Chromatic Choosability of Complete Multipartite Graphs with Small Partite Sets
papers.abstract: Chromatic choosability is a notion of fundamental importance in list coloring. A graph is chromatic-choosable when its chromatic number is equal to its list chromatic number. In their 1979 paper on list coloring, Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor showed that complete $m$-partite graphs with every partite set of size 2, denoted by $K_{2*m}$, are chromatic-choosable. In 1990, Kostochka and Sidorenko introduced the list color function of a graph $G$, denoted by $P_{\ell}(G,m)$, which is the list analogue of the chromatic polynomial of $G$, $P(G,m)$. A graph $G$ is enumeratively chromatic-choosable when $P_{\ell}(G,m) = P(G,m)$ whenever $m \in \mathbb{N}$. In this paper, we explore the question as to whether $K_{2*m}$ satisfies this stronger property. We establish a recursive lower bound on $P_{\ell}(K_{2*m},m)$ and prove that $K_{2*3}$ and $K_{2*4}$ are weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable, meaning that equality holds at the chromatic number. We also develop a general lower bound for the list color function of certain joins with complete graphs and use it to prove that $K_p\vee K_{2*5}$ is weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable whenever $p\geq 15$, and that $K_p\vee K_{2,2,3}$ is weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable whenever $p\geq 3$. These results provide progress toward a weaker form of a conjecture of Allred and Mudrock concerning the enumerative chromatic choosability of complete graph joins.

papers.title: Kleinian groups with tunnel number one
papers.abstract: We give a structural theory for the holonomy groups of hyperbolic links with tunnel number 1 in arbitrary 3-manifolds. This is a first step towards understanding the canonical triangulations of such links, as it generalises the combinatorial structure theory of two-bridge link groups that is an input to the Sakuma--Weeks triangulation.

papers.title: MagTrace: Tracing magnetic order through the evolving scientific literature
papers.abstract: Much of the research on magnetic materials starts from their magnetic order, but confirming it from the papers by hand can take hours, and curated databases can be incomplete and outdated. In this work, we build MagTrace, a language model agent that, given only a material's name, searches four literature databases, reads open access full text and reports the magnetic orders the current literature supports, each with a confidence score and citations a reader can check. We evaluate its performance on 18 materials against an answer key complied from published papers, compared with two other conditions that vary in level of retrieval. On a score from 0 to 1 that combines correctness, detail, whether the most confident order is current, and citation integrity, MagTrace scores 0.839; the same underlying language model scores 0.676 given the abstracts from one literature search and 0.548 answering from memory. With a single search, the model finds the right kind of order but omits the propagation vector, which describes how the pattern repeats through the material's crystal structure, in 85% of its orders. From memory, the model often cites titles that lead to no indexed paper (for 25% of the orders we could check), and when a cited paper exists and has an abstract, the abstract contradicts the claim for 17% of those citations, against 7% for MagTrace.

papers.title: Computability of states and non-computability of traces
papers.abstract: We study computable presentations of the state space and trace space of computably presented C*-algebras. We show that the state space has a computably compact presentation with respect to which the evaluation of states is a computable map. As an application of having computable states, we obtain a computable version of the GNS construction. We show that the trace space does not share these computational properties. Specifically, we give an example of a computable presentation of a simple AF algebra for which the trace space has no computably compact presentation with respect to which evaluation is computable. As a consequence, we demonstrate that the Elliott invariant of a computably presentable classifiable C*-algebra is not always presentable in a way that makes all key features of the invariant computable.

papers.title: Alignment under Hard Negative Re-Pairing: Cross-Modal Similarity, Scale and Retrieval
papers.abstract: Do vision and language models represent the world alike? That question hides three: what structure each modality has, whether the two modalities organize images and their captions alike, and whether a model ranks an image's own caption highly. Centered kernel alignment (CKA) and neighborhood agreement answer the second, yet matching and model selection use them as if they identified individual pairs and answered the third. To test this reading, we introduce hard negative re-pairing: every image receives the caption of a similar image, and nothing else changes. Although no image keeps its own caption and annotators judge a majority of the substituted captions wrong, CKA stays higher than under a random re-pairing that keeps 80% of the original pairs. In all 22 image-text models we test, neighborhood agreement loses far less than top-one retrieval, which collapses. The reason is scale: these diagnostics pool over many neighbors, matching and retrieval are decided among the nearest ones, and an exact decomposition shows that near-neighbor pairs contribute almost nothing to CKA. In the matching problems we test, an exact maximizer of CKA would not return the original pairing. On COCO and Flickr30k, the model with the highest diagnostic value retrieves worse on held-out data than the model chosen by validation recall, even where the two correlate positively. What re-pairing removes is the informative part: that share tracks retrieval on both datasets and ranks encoder pairs before alignment training. A diagnostic should be reported with its question and its scale, and tested against hard negative re-pairing.

papers.title: TabK: Amortized Bayesian Estimation of the Number of Clusters in Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Estimating the number of clusters, $k$, is a fundamental prerequisite for most clustering algorithms. Traditionally, this estimation has relied on computationally expensive grid searches over internal cluster validity indices (CVIs) or adaptive clustering algorithms, both constrained by specific statistical assumptions. We introduce TabK, a zero-shot, permutation-invariant transformer architecture that frames the estimation of $k$ as an amortized Bayesian inference problem for tabular data. TabK leverages a novel Quantile Feature Encoder (QFE) to extract position-free, content-derived representations from empirical marginal distributions. By learning a generalized structural bias over a diverse synthetic prior, TabK estimates the number of clusters in a single forward pass per ensemble member. Evaluated across 50 diverse real-world benchmarks, TabK outperforms all competing methods, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) value of 1.04 compared to 2.14 for the closest competitor. TabK also achieves the lowest average inference time, producing estimates in less than one second on average and running $2\times$ faster than TabClustPFN and $30\times$ faster than traditional CVIs such as Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz. Code is available at https://github.com/mrbakhtyari/TabK.

papers.title: The FRB Population Revisited: Rate, Energy, Evolution, and Host-DM Constraints from the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
papers.abstract: We present a study that simultaneously fits for key fast radio burst (FRB) population properties using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog while calibrating for instrumental selection effects. Our inferred volumetric rate at $z=0$ is $1.1^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\times 10^{5}\,{\rm Gpc}^{-3}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ above an isotropic-equivalent energy of $10^{39}$ erg and below a scattering timescale of 30 ms at 600 MHz. The evolution of the FRB rate relative to the cosmic star formation rate remains statistically unconstrained. Assuming a Schechter function for the energy distribution, isotropic emission, and 1-GHz emission bandwidth, we find a characteristic maximum energy of $2.0^{+2.6}_{-1.0} \times 10^{41}$ erg and a differential power-law index of $-1.41\,^{+0.27}_{-0.21}({\rm stat.})\,\pm\,0.35({\rm sys.})$. The host galaxy contribution to the observed dispersion measure (DM) is modeled as a log-normal distribution; assuming a total Galactic contribution of 80 $\text{pc cm}^{-3}$, we find a median host-galaxy DM contribution of $199^{+34}_{-36}\;\text{pc cm}^{-3}$ in the rest-frame. Finally, we find that the average FRB spectrum, described by a spectral index of $α=-1.0^{+0.5}_{-0.6}$, is inconsistent with being flat at the $\sim2σ$ level. We note an excess of high-S/N bursts at low DMs in the observed sample that is not predicted by the best-fit model. Testing alternative models does not alleviate this tension; future population studies may mitigate this limitation by incorporating robust fluence and redshift measurements.

papers.title: Bayesian Image Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Three-Photon Positronium Ratio Imaging: Toward Radiotheranostic Applications
papers.abstract: Three-photon annihilation imaging can estimate positronium decay ratios with pure positron emitters, including the imaging agents of radiotheranostic pairs, but quantitative reconstruction is limited by heterogeneous localization errors, selection-dependent sensitivity, and background coincidences. We develop a Bayesian reconstruction combining a three-dimensional event-response model with a Poisson likelihood and latent signal-background allocations. Photon-energy and interaction-position uncertainties enter the event covariance; a simulation-calibrated scale mixture accommodates heavy-tailed errors. Posterior sampling gives credible intervals for the three-to-two-photon enhancement ratio. We compare kernel deposition, voxel MLEM, and matched regional maximum likelihood. At 3000 selected events in full-absorption simulation, the regional Bayesian estimator had ratio RMSE 0.067, versus 0.075 for kernel-deposition region-of-interest analysis. In a transport-based four-rod simulation without background, biases averaged at most 3.2% over six independent simulations, whereas background and detector mismatch degraded it. In a measured uniform phantom, the heavy-tailed regional model gave 1.02, 0.74, 1.02 for the 2, 3, 4 mm rods (5 mm reference; nominal 1). Matched regional maximum likelihood agreed with the Bayesian estimates in every simulated setting (bias differences within 0.15 points) and on the measured data (within 0.008), so gains derive from the regional likelihood. Under Poisson Kullback-Leibler loss, Gamma posterior means dominate maximum likelihood, appreciably only at small counts; horseshoe-type and smoothing priors changed voxel images but not regional ratios, whereas shrinking ratios across regions reduced error when regions shared a ratio. Posterior intervals quantify the uncertainty that treatment decisions require; calibration and background modeling remain limiting.

papers.title: GlaucomaMarker - Biomarker-Grounded Glaucoma Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness. In the current clinical setting, glaucoma diagnosis is generally conducted by assessing optic disc cupping and asymmetry. Vision-language models (VLMs) have been utilized in recent years for glaucoma, mostly trained on fixed templates or AI-generated captions, as no public text describes the biomarkers. Our proposed framework, GlaucomaMarker, hypothesizes that retinal structural biomarkers can ground glaucoma-based VLMs. It converts public segmentation masks into sentences describing eleven biomarkers, to teach retinal foundation models to read them. We applied this framework to RETFound (GlaucomaMarker-R) and FLAIR (GlaucomaMarker-F), training on 9,778 images that yielded 45,190 image-text pairs. On a real-world clinical cohort, GlaucomaMarker-F detects glaucoma with an AUROC of 0.905, against 0.848 for FLAIR, and both read the biomarkers where baselines stay near random guessing. Since the biomarker text is computed from existing masks, it comes at no extra cost.

papers.title: Decision models for UAVBench and the viability of edge deployment
papers.abstract: Small language models are often proposed for reasoning onboard a drone. However, a good benchmark score does not tell us whether a model will actually run, and run usefully, on an edge computer. In this paper we study three related questions using the UAV decision benchmark, UAVBench. First, are small structured decision models good candidates for these tasks? Second, can an ordinary local machine (a Mac) screen candidate models before we test them on physical devices? Third, what software and resource limits govern deployment? Our main Mac evaluation covers 24 model configurations on the same 2,000 validated multiple-choice questions from UAVBench. These include 20 size-and-precision configurations of 11 generative models, plus four open-weight structured decision models that received no additional UAVBench-specific training. A structured decision model, H2O Lightning 4B, achieved the highest accuracy we observed, scoring 77.65% on the Mac. This shows that these models are well suited to this kind of task. However, when we tried to deploy the decision models, we ran into conversion and runtime limits on the edge devices we tested, which we describe in detail. To test local screening, we ran matched evaluations of two generative models on both the Mac and a Qualcomm RB3 board. The accuracies did not match exactly, but the ranking did. LFM2 2.6B ranked above Qwen2.5 1.5B on both platforms. This supports using a local machine to shortlist candidates. That said, individual answers still differed between platforms, so testing on the actual hardware remained necessary.

papers.title: Sharp Estimates for Jacobi Heat Kernels on a Ball and on a Simplex in the Full Range of Parameters
papers.abstract: We establish genuinely sharp heat-kernel estimates for orthogonal expansions on the Euclidean unit ball and on the unit simplex throughout their natural parameter ranges. For the ball weight $W_μ(x)=(1-\|x\|^2)^{μ-1/2}$, we extend the known estimate from the range $μ\geq0$ to every $μ>-1/2$. For the simplex, we prove the corresponding estimate for every $κ\in(-1/2,\infty)^{d+1}$. The estimates retain exactly the form known in the classical ranges. The proof is based on analytic continuation of the classical product and reduction formulas. Below the integrability threshold, the ball formula decomposes into an endpoint term and a derivative correction, while the simplex formula produces endpoint and mixed-derivative terms indexed by the negative coordinates. In the lowest simplex parameter range we use the auxiliary even ultraspherical kernel introduced by Nowak, Sjögren, and Szarek.

papers.title: Bivariant $K$-theory for bornological algebras
papers.abstract:
We construct a presentable, stable \(\infty\)-category \( KK\), and exhibit it as the target of the universal functor from the category of bornological algebras into cocomplete, stable \(\infty\)-categories, preserving filtered colimits, and satisfying smooth homotopy invariance, excision, and stabilisation with respect to Schatten-class or smooth compact operators. We also construct a bivariant \(K\)-theory \(
KK\) for suitably nuclear bornological algebras, and show that it is a right Bousfield localisation of \( KK\). The category \(
KK\) is symmetric monoidal and admits a bivariant Chern character to local cyclic homology. The categories \(
KK\) and \( KK\) corepresent Cortiñas and Thom's diffeotopy \(K\)-theory. We use the Chern character to show that up to a suitable Schatten-class stabilisation, the complexified Chern character from the diffeotopy \(K\)-theory (resp. \(K\)-homology) of a smooth manifold to the compactly supported cohomology (resp. locally finite homology) of the manifold is an isomorphism.

papers.title: Effective Hamiltonians and asymptotic band coupling
papers.abstract: By a multiple-scale asymptotic expansion, we derive effective macroscopic models for a large class of tight-binding Schrödinger equations with slow spatial variations. For wave packets that are spectrally localized to some point $(K;E) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$ in the unperturbed tight-binding dispersion relation, our effective models produce long-time approximations of the tight-binding dynamics, accurate to any prescribed order in the asymptotic parameter. Our framework allows the point $(K;E)$ to be degenerate, meaning that multiple (but not necessarily all) energy bands of the tight-binding Hamiltonian can attain the value $E$ at the frequency $K$. We construct an effective Hamiltonian on the relevant degenerate subspace, which quantifies the coupling between the degenerate and other bands. Several applications and numerical simulations illustrate the theory.

papers.title: AV-FLARE: Feature-Level Reliability Estimation for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MMER) systems typically rely on learned feature representations and attention mechanisms that implicitly weight information across time and modalities. However, these mechanisms do not explicitly incorporate input reliability, despite the presence of noise in audio, occlusions in visual data, and the sparse and event-driven nature of affective cues. We propose AV-FLARE, a framework that explicitly estimates fine-grained reliability scores across both temporal and feature dimensions prior to temporal modeling and uses them to modulate feature representations. Reliability is computed using two complementary components: (i) a supervised network trained jointly with the classification objective, and (ii) an unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Model that models global feature distributions. These signals are combined to provide both task-driven and distribution-aware reliability estimates. To integrate modalities, we introduce a hierarchical cross-modal attention mechanism in which textual features are used to guide audio-visual fusion as a semantic reference modality. Experiments on the IEMOCAP dataset show that AV-FLARE improves over a no-reliability baseline, achieving 90.81\% accuracy and 81.69\% F1-score, corresponding to gains of +4.41% and +8.56%, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating explicit input reliability estimation may improve robustness in multimodal emotion recognition under the evaluated setting.

papers.title: Nehari type characterizations of the mountain pass level on cones
papers.abstract: We relate the mountain pass level of a functional to its infimum over the part of the Nehari set formed by local maximizers of the fiber maps. {Unlike in the classical setting where every fiber map has a unique global maximizer,} the fiber maps need not all have a maximizer: working on each path-connected component of the cone of directions where they do, we show that the two levels coincide, for merely continuous functionals and without any compactness assumption. We also introduce a notion of mountain pass geometry with respect to a cone, which may hold when the classical one fails. {This geometry includes the zero-level case when a suitable separating set exists.} Under the Palais--Smale condition, each component carries a critical point at its own mountain pass level. Applications include indefinite and concave-convex problems with sign-changing weights, the affine $p$-Laplacian, nonlocal problems, and a problem related to the Fuč\'ık spectrum.

papers.title: Distant Bell States via Measured Spin Chain Dynamics
papers.abstract: Preparing distant qubits in Bell states is a core requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum computation. The nonequilibrium unitary dynamics of spin chains have been envisaged as a convenient quantum channel for intra-chip communications. Typically it establishes mixed entangled states between its remote ends, to be purified by entanglement distillation after several uses of the channel to obtain Bell states. Here we show how the establishment of entanglement via spin chain dynamics can be (a) sped up and (b) made to yield a pure entangled state after a single usage of the channel, which is upgradable to a Bell-state without the complexity of purification. To this end, we intersperse unitary evolution for some period with measurements on intermediary spins. We explore two different measurements: a measurement that post-selects for a ground state; and local measurements in the computational basis. We illustrate the mechanism with qubits coupled to the ends of a 1D $XY$ spin chain.

papers.title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
papers.abstract: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

papers.title: The Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model at isospin density in closed form: what a regularization can change
papers.abstract: At zero temperature, the mean-field thermodynamic potential of the two-flavour Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model at isospin chemical potential reduces to a divergent momentum integral of two quasiparticle levels. In practice this integral is cut off at momenta not far above the chemical potentials being probed. We evaluate it exactly, at an arbitrary cutoff, using the Hermite reduction. The result is an algebraic boundary term and three incomplete elliptic integrals, one of each kind. Their modulus, parameter and amplitude at the end of the path are fixed by the triangle formed by the two levels at zero momentum. The power divergences reside in the boundary term, while the remaining divergence is logarithmic: the momentum axis is an open path on an elliptic curve, and the ultraviolet is the puncture at which it ends. The closed form makes the role of regularization explicit. As the cutoff is removed, sharp and smooth cutoffs acting on the momentum alone differ only by an additive constant and by two terms that the vacuum inputs fix. The medium separation scheme reproduces the resulting potential up to an additive constant. By contrast, a cutoff applied separately to the two levels generates an isospin density below the onset of condensation and violates the Silver Blaze property. The closed form gives the state that continues the vacuum along the isospin axis without numerical momentum integration. With the same vacuum fit, a cutoff kept finite gives a visibly different state. The two differ by explicit terms that vanish only as the cutoff is removed: they are different models, not two regularizations of one.

papers.title: Moment-Based Transient Network Models for Finite-Strain Viscoelasticity
papers.abstract: A viscoelastic framework is developed through a moment reduction of the hereditary integral defining the free energy of transient polymer networks. Expanding the chain energy about the mean history invariant produces a hierarchy of tensorial moments representing the network formation history. For energies depending on the relative first invariant, the leading approximation recovers Lubliner's model, providing a physical interpretation of its second-rank history tensor as an average of the inverse deformation metrics at chain formation. The next approximation introduces a fourth-rank tensor that accounts for variability among formation configurations. These moments admit equivalent rate forms and efficient recurrence relations, while their evolution permits the establishment of sufficient conditions for dissipation. Comparisons with an exact hereditary representation of the three-term Arruda-Boyce energy demonstrate that the first-moment approximation captures the overall response, while retaining the second moment improves accuracy, particularly under complex loading histories. We also incorporate non-exponential relaxation through distributed detachment kinetics described by the Kohlrausch-Williams-Watts (KWW) function. Assuming thermorheological simplicity, calibration to thermally accelerated butyl-rubber relaxation measurements yields excellent agreement across wide ranges of time and temperature. The calibrated continuous rate spectrum is then discretized into a finite Prony series using equal-probability bins.
